VIA RAIL
subsubtopic: PLANS TO CANCEL SERVICE IN ALBERTA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope I will have the same good luck with my motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
VIA Rail is planning to cancel rail service on the Edmonton-Jasper-Vancouver run which is an essential part of the historic link in transcontinental service. Further, rail service to Drum-heller will be cancelled, and to Prince Rupert reduced. Since this would be an incomprehensible act economically damaging a trading area of one million people, and which represents a growth area second to none in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert):
That the cabinet, under Section 64 of the National Transportation Act, direct VIA Rail to conduct public hearings before any reduction in present rail service is imposed on Edmonton, an act that would have the gravest repercussions on the attitude of northern Albertans maintaining a sense of national unity.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Postal employees were given the legal right to strike in 1967. Since then there have been 12 strikes, almost one every year. That in itself tells us quite clearly something is wrong, that the government has failed to co-operate with management and labour to make it work, instead hoping problems will go away by dumping them onto a Crown corporation. The current postal dispute is now in its eleventh day. The government has failed to provide leadership and management. The strike is causing very, very serious hardship for many Canadians. Therefore, Madam Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko):
That this House urge the government to take these problems seriously and to live up to its responsibilities and obligations by either negotiating in good faith or legislating the striking employees back to work.

IMPERIAL OIL PROJECT AT COLD LAKE, ALTA.-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Yesterday's cancellation of the $12 billion Cold Lake project is the largest single casualty of the Liberal energy program to date. Until now the minister has been able to ignore, or has ignored, the 165 rigs which have left the country. He has ignored the 20 to 30 per cent drop in employment in the service industry in the west. He has ignored the large increase in imports. However, he cannot ignore the cancellation of a $12 billion project. The national interest is seriously at stake. Since this decision resulted directly from the impasse between the federal government and the province of Alberta, and is also related directly to elements of the National Energy Program, what action is the minister proposing to take since both of those reasons are within his control?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: IMPERIAL OIL PROJECT AT COLD LAKE, ALTA.-GOVERNMENT POSITION

Madam Speaker, the hon. member must have spent the morning priming his rhetoric, but I wish it were accurate. There has been no cancellation of the Cold Lake project. The project is delayed until an agreement is reached between the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada. The company expressed its intention to proceed with the project if there is a satisfactory agreement between the two governments, which both governments are hoping for. As a matter of fact the statement says, "We will reassess our position on the Cold Lake project as soon as a federal-provincial agreement is reached". Therefore there is no cancellation.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the casual attitude of the minister is just incomprehensible. This is a $12 billion project which will affect all of the country. I cannot understand the minister sitting there and saying it is just suspended, it will get started again. It will take two years to get it going again. The cancellation of this project will, in 1990, result in an increase in imports of about 10 per cent, or $2 billion a year at current prices. It will result in economic opportunity lost in Ontario and Quebec. About 30 to 35 per cent of the cost of the project will be spent in those parts of the country. The minister has a responsibility to all Canadians to get these projects going. Will the minister call a meeting with Mr. Leitch at the earliest possible date to press for a conclusion of these negotiations in order to avoid further failures such as the cancellation of the Alsands project? Having meetings once a month or every couple of months is just not good enough. We have to get this project going.

Second, Mr. Leitch and I have agreed that we should meet in the latter part of July or the early part of August. We have both agreed that this is the most convenient and appropriate time to do so. The president of Imperial Oil has been advised of this situation, and he recognizes better than my friend that these difficult negotiations cannot be resolved just by a meeting called suddenly. There is a lot of work to be done.
I have proposed in the past that we try to resolve the issue of the tar sands independently for the other, more difficult issues which are still dividing us, but the government of Alberta has taken the view that there should be a global settlement and not a settlement only on the tar sands.
There is not much more I can do in that sense to speed up a resolution of this issue other than to keep on working at it and to hope that we will arrive at a satisfactory arrangement for Canadian consumers as well as the industry.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday concerning the question of the uranium cartel there were many important questions pertaining to the legality of that issue. There is an equally important question concerning ministerial responsibility. I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question following a quotation from a former Prime Minister on the nature of ministerial responsibility who said that a minister of the Crown is responsible, under the system in Great Britain or Canada, for the minutest details of the administration in his department; he is politically responsible, but he does not know anything at all about them, and that when anything goes wrong in his department he is responsible therefor to Parliament. MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   COMBINES URANIUM CARTEL-ALLEGED FAILURE OF MR. TRUDEAU TO EXERCISE RESPONSIBILITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move a motion for the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the failure of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to exercise his responsibilities in the serious question of potential ministerial culpability in the establishment of a uranium cartel in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   COMBINES URANIUM CARTEL-ALLEGED FAILURE OF MR. TRUDEAU TO EXERCISE RESPONSIBILITIES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) has given me notice under the terms of Standing Order 26 of his intention to move the adjournment of the House to discuss the alleged failure by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) "to exercise his responsibilities in the establishment of a uranium cartel in Canada".
It seems to the Chair that the hon. member's motion is couched in the terms of a non-confidence motion in the Prime Minister, which is not envisaged by the provisions of Standing Order 26. I need not quote any rulings by my predecessors as hon. members are aware that there are ample precedents to this effect.
Furthermore, the motion raises a substantive matter which can only be dealt with by a distinct motion after due notice. In my view, the motion relates to the conduct of a minister and to that extent it is excluded from the operation of Standing Order 26. I refer hon. members to Section 16(f) of the Standing Order, and I quote:
-the discussion under the motion must not raise any question which, according to the Standing Orders of the House, can only be debated on a distinct motion under notice.
In other words, the motion is essentially of the nature of a censure motion and as a substantive motion it cannot be considered under the provisions of Standing Order 26.
I might add that the logic of this rule is that it would be unfair for the members or the ministers concerned to have their conduct debated under a motion to adjourn the House rather than a specific motion dealing with the substantive question upon which a decision could be taken by the House.
A motion pursuant to Standing Order 26 is not subject to a decision by the House; it is merely a vehicle for debate. Even if it were subject to a decision by the House, the decision would only be as to whether or not the House was to adjourn. Therefore, I cannot allow the debate under Standing Order 26.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-83, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act, the Salaries Act, the Parliamentary Secretaries Act and the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Madam Speaker, today the House is studying a bill aimed at raising the salaries of members of Parliament. Some people will say that the timing is wrong, but there can never be a right moment! We are always expected to study and solve only the problems of the nation. The public always forgets that we are men and women who of course accept this difficult and demanding way of life but who must also look after their family and be able to lead a decent life. Above all, the public forgets that our institutions force them to shoulder the much heavier responsibility of having to vote for themselves the salary they will be paid. It may look like a marvellous freedom, but in fact it is a thankless task which no one other than parliamentarians can do in their stead. The last time the salaries and allowances of members of Parliament were examined was in 1974. And if I may make a short review, Mr. Speaker, it will be readily understood why a salary increase has now become urgent and absolutely necessary.
In 1974, members of Parliament wanted to raise their salary because they considered that they were paid less than the amount to which they might have been entitled. A group of members from both sides of the House was then formed to
July 9, 1981

examine the subject and make recommendations. After a serious study, that committee came to the conclusion that the salaries of parliamentarians ought to be 50 per cent higher than what they were on July 8, 1974. The committee also recommended a certain adjustment formula applicable on an annual basis. Then there was a debate in this House and, since those recommendations had been made by members of Parliament who happened to be directly concerned with the issue, after a rather lengthy debate it was finally concluded that there had to be a still deeper cut so that parliamentarians ended up with roughly 30 per cent instead of the 50 per cent hike which had been deemed to be the acceptable minimum.
Mr. Speaker, we are caught in a sort of vicious circle. Every time the issue of higher salaries for members of Parliament comes up, we always want, because of the delicate situation I have just mentioned, that parliamentarians themselves introduce the appropriate legislation to be able to catch up so that we will not have to seek substantial raises in the future. However, since we are always ill at ease to endorse the full recommendations made to us by commissions of members of Parliament, we never did manage to catch up so as to get the minimum recommended by those study groups. On the contrary, we always drop lower and thus aggravate the problem and make it even more difficult a few years later to make the adjustments which by then have become more than necessary. That is what happened once again in 1975 when finally, after a long debate, we reached a compromise so that the increase was only about 30 per cent, not the 50 per cent which had been recommended, and there has been no increase since.
I would add also that this 30 per cent adjustment, which was decided on by way of compromise, was to be equivalent to the industrial composite up to a maximum of 7 per cent. Now we all know that 7 per cent was substantially less than the actual increase in the cost of living and in the industrial composite. Since 1975, members have only received 30 or 33 per cent of what was then considered a basic minimum. Their allowance was not indexed but was adjusted to a rate which was out of line with reality, that is a maximum of 7 per cent; not only that, but for two years, under the Anti-Inflation Board, there was absolutely no yearly adjustment. So in real terms, since the 1975 increase which was retroactive to July 8, 1974, members received only a 30 per cent increase compared to the 50 per cent which was recommended, and an average year adjustment of 4.4 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, these are the facts which must objectively and honestly be made public and understood by those who might be tempted to criticize members on both sides of the House for considering after six years, or rather six and a half years, a reasonable and decent salary adjustment. What happened also, and I think it is appropriate to mention this, is that in 1975, when a compromise was reached to limit ourselves to one third or 30 per cent and 7 per cent, which actually became 4.4 per cent because of the two lost years which I mentioned, was that
Senate and House of Commons Act a section, Section 34(7) I believe, was added to the act so that in the future members would not be put in the awkward position of using their own recommendations as a basis. The act will include a provision so that the government of the day will refer the issue of parliamentarians' salaries to an independent commission; that in fact was what made members accept the compromise despite the fact that they found the 30 per cent increase unsatisfactory and the 7 per cent yearly adjustment laughable. But members bought this deal in 1975 because they believed that four or five years down the road, after the next election, there would be an independent commission established under the statutes of Canada, which would review the issue of parliamentary salaries and report to the government within six months after its appointment, and the commission itself was to be established two months after the election.
The members took that for granted and that is in fact what happened. There was a provision included in the legislation and the facts show that after the 1979 election, under the act, under this statutory obligation, a commission was established, the Hales Commission. The commission did report within six months; however, when it did report, another election had taken place. We all know that there were two closely held elections. Therefore, the government, under a statutory obligation, set up another independent commission, the Mclsaac-Balcer Commission, to review the salaries paid to parliamentarians, in the light of the Hales report which was produced in due time but which could not be implemented because of these two successive elections. The important thing to note now, as I am speaking to you today, is that the report of this independent commission established under the statutes of the land has been produced and tabled by the government. I had the opportunity to table that report in December last, and it is precisely that kind of report of an independent commission analysing responsibly and objectively, fair-mindedly and without any conflict of interests, the conditions of members compared to other sectors of economic activity in Canada. It is precisely on that kind of report that the legislation now under consideration is based.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, as I said, the last major increase in compensation for MPs and senators was made under an act to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act, the Salaries Act and the Parliamentary Secretaries Act, passed in May, 1975, retroactive to July 8, 1974. This act introduced an annual adjustment formula based on the industrial composite, but limited to a maximum of 7 per cent.
The 1975 amendment added Section 34(7) to the Senate and House of Commons Act. This subsection stipulates that within two months after the date fixed for return of the writs at each general election, the governor in council shall appoint commissioners to inquire into the adequacy of the annual variations of sessional allowances payable to MPs and sena-

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act
tors, and to report thereon to the governor in council, with such recommendations as they consider appropriate, within six months after the time of their appointment.
In August, 1979, Mr. Speaker, the government appointed Mr. Hales a commissioner under Section 34(7). His report was tabled in Parliament April 23, 1980. No substantive action was taken by the government on this report as another commission had to be set up because of the last election. On May 9, 1980 under Section 34(7) the governor in council set up a commission composed of Dr. J. Clifford Mclsaac as chairman, and the Hon. Leon Balcer. The new commission took Mr. Hales' report into account, and its report was tabled in Parliament on December 2, 1980.
On April 30, 1980, the subcommittee on matters pertaining to members, staff, staff allowances, constituency offices and members' pensions, salaries and allowances recommended that severance pay be given to a member of Parliament who is not re-elected and that the MPs pension plan be modified. The Mclsaac-Balcer report deals with the whole subject and some aspects of it are excellent. It is based on logical and specific arguments, and it draws on extensive and pertinent information to support its recommendations. Most important, it is the first time in history that we can base such legislation on a report made by an independent commission based on the statutes of the land.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I said that the purpose of the bill is to increase the salaries of parliamentarians, but allow me to be more specific. It would be misleading to focus our discussion on a mere percentage increase. Indeed, the thing is to set the salaries of parliamentarians and to figure out the compensation to which they are entitled. The Canadian people want to be represented and governed by the most consistent and devoted people. They do not want politics to be the privilege of those of independent means and they want above all that those who make decisions affecting our collective future to remain financially independent. The sessional allowance, Mr. Speaker, because the legislation carefully refrains from referring to salaries, is designed to allow the member to live decently but not in luxury, so that he may devote himself to state matters. The member gives up his private life. He has often to keep two houses between which he travels most of the year. No one surely goes into politics to become rich, but no one should ruin himself either in the process. Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to note yesterday the comments made by leaders in their respective sectors in Canada. They are not parliamentarians and had nothing to say about the advisability of legislation designed to increase the salaries of parliamentarians.
I was pleased to see that union leaders favored such an increase, and made very interesting comments in support of the case of hon. members who have not had any salary increase for six years and a half and who have only received a yearly adjustment of 4.4 percent for seven years. They recognized that was a case of glaring injustice and that there was a
danger that hon. members or people in general would take no further interest in public life, and that we might end up by having here only people who are very well-off, excluding those who have to leave their businesses or professions behind, who have a low income, because parliamentary life is too exacting and the salary is inadequate. Let me briefly read the comments of three of those people, quoting from an article which appeared yesterday on page 8 of The Gazette under the title: [English]
Canada's MPs need a raise, panel agrees.
The first one who was asked about this is Mr. Dennis McDermott, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress. He said:
There are a lot of talented people out there who are not individually wealthy and who are not professionals and who are probably not running because they cannot afford to. A raise might attract them.
It is a very demanding job. And what you have now is the spectacle of some independently rich people treating it as some sort of game.
Louis Laberge, a well known person in Quebec, head of the powerful Quebec Federation of Labour, in the same article of yesterday's Gazette is quoted as saying about the need for a raise for MPs:
I have lived through quite a few governments-and I intend to keep doing so-I'm more useful to governments and my members where I am-but if you want people who know what they are talking about and who will devote their time then you've got to pay them.
The timing-there's never a proper time. They should do it now.
There are ten people quoted, but I will only quote one more. As opposed to the union sector, I will deal with the small business sector. Businessman John Bulloch, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, is quoted as saying:
But their whole job is a social disaster-late hours, travel, unfair demands. Their personal life is a nightmare-I would give them more, of course-they should get an extra $20,000 in harassment pay.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I was happy to see that at last leaders of opinion in this country have realized and support the need for a decent raise for members of Parliament.
As I was saying, our salaries have been increased by only 30 per cent when they should have been increased by 50 per cent over the last seven years to catch up. We have received an average annual adjustment of 4.4 per cent in the last seven years; no worker in the country has suffered that treatment. This is why I can understand that Mr. McDermott, Mr. Laberge and Mr. Bulloch speak so loudly in our favour. [Translation]
The Mclsaac-Balcer report, Mr. Speaker, recommended a minimum of $45,000 a year for each hon. member in recognition of the demands of his duties, the very long working hours and the necessity to be both in Ottawa to discuss the problems of Canada, and in his riding to listen to his constituents' concerns. The government has very seriously and for a long time considered the recommendations in the report. The increases in the bill could come into effect from July 1, 1980.
July 9, 1981

As a matter of fact, the Mclsaac-Balcer report considered the salaries as of January 1, 1980, and it would be unfair if the delays which were necessary to draft that bill were to postpone the implementation of these legitimate recommendations.
Mr. Speaker, the government, the majority of members on this side of the House, most members of the Progressive Conservative Party and most members of the NDP to-day recommend that we take only two thirds of the increases suggested in the Mclsaac-Balcer report, even though, in the last seven years, parliamentarians have received much lower salary increases than those received by many of their constituents, and even though they have had only a ridiculous average annual adjustment of 4.4 per cent. Mr. Speaker, I have here a chart which shows what has been the salary of parliamentarians in the last ten years, from 1971 to 1981, in relation to the consumer price index, the composite industrial index and the manufacturing sector. It is important that people know to what extent those who govern this country, those who try to improve the situation in this country, those who aim only at improving the welfare of their fellow citizens, have lacked in self-indulgence and to what extent what they have obtained in the last few years has been less than what ordinary citizens have received on the average.
Mr. Speaker, if we compare the salary increases for members of Parliament in the last ten years to the consumer price index, we note a difference of 40 per cent. Over ten years, we have received 40 per cent less than the consumer price index increase in Canada. I know of no worker in my constituency, and there is probably none in Canada, who has received wage increases 40 per cent lower than the increase in the consumer price index. Yet this is the case of Canadian parliamentarians, and I am speaking about federal parliamentarians, Mr. Speaker, not of those of Ontario, British Columbia or Quebec, who, as we know, have different salaries which are in certain cases much higher than ours.
If we compare the salary increases of parliamentarians since 1971, that is for the last ten years, to the composite industrial index, the difference is no longer 40 per cent, but rather 55 per cent. This means that organized workers have on the average, over the last ten years received 55 per cent more in increases than we have. If we compare our salary-and this is important-to industrial wages in Canada, the difference is 75 per cent. This is completely ridiculous; it is outrageous! And I could add that the difference between our own increases and those of postal workers, for instance, for whom I have the figures here, is even worse, as much as 85 per cent. Over the last ten years, postal workers' salary increases have been 85 per cent higher than parliamentarians.
What we are proposing today is that we accept two thirds of the increase recommended in our own conciliation report, because we, members of Parliament, do not have the privilege to negotiate a collective agreement every year. We are subject to an act which provides for a review of our salaries by an
Senate and House of Commons Act
independent commission every four or five years. However, this is the first time in our history that an independent commission presents a report as required under the act, and we are not even accepting 100 per cent of what is recommended in this report, in what might be called a conciliation report. We are accepting only two thirds. I challenge any worker in Canada to accept only two thirds of the increase recommended in a conciliation report. This has never happened in the past, and we do so today in spite of the fact that we are now 40 per cent behind the increase in the cost of living index, 55 per cent behind the composite industrial index, 75 per cent behind the manufacturing sector and 85 per cent behind postal workers' salary increases. Then again, only two thirds of the conciliation report is reflected in the bill before us today.
Mr. Speaker, if I get worked up at this point, it is because when I had to study that report, I understood why Messrs. Mclsaac and Balcer were offended by the present. When they made comparisons with workers in other sectors, with industrial workers, with workers in the manufacturing sector, when they analysed the cost of living, when they considered the salaries paid in the public service, I understood why many people in this country do not respect the members of Parliament. We should start by setting an example and respecting ourselves. I feel that what is proposed in this report is a decent minimum and once again, it is thanks to the good faith and the good will of members of the three parties in this House that we agreed to introduce this bill that will be voted on tonight at 9:45. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying that this is indeed so and that we have agreed to say publicly that it is as a result of an agreement among the three parties that we proceed in this manner. It is an agreement made not only with the Progressive Conservatives but also with the New Democrats.
Petitions have been signed by a majority of members from each party, a very substantial majority of each party, on the issue of pensions. A petition has been signed by a majority of Liberal and Progressive Conservative members on the salary issue, and the New Democratic Party assured us that a majority of their members support all the provisions of this bill, including those on salaries. We have their assurance that a majority of their members will vote in favour of this bill tonight, and these were the conditions under which we have decided and agreed to introduce this bill that I am now discussing. So let it be quite clear that this is not a unilateral move on the part of the government. The need was so obvious, the injustice so blatant that for the first time, I think, in a spontaneous manner, we were able to win a substantial majority in each caucus to restore some order and bring to a decent minimum the salaries of parliamentarians. I am grateful to the two opposition House leaders, my colleague for Nepean-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker) and my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who both spoke in good faith for their respective caucus and negotiated the agreement which will enable Parliament to implement two

retirement allowances to parliamentarians receiving a salary for extra responsibilities.
As far as the retirement pension allowance or pension is concerned, clearly no comparison can be made with pensions paid in the private sector. Such a comparison cannot hold, for the simple reason that in order to serve in this House, the overwhelming majority of members have to jeopardize, and very often indeed cut themselves off from their profession, business or other occupation. This is a unique feature of parliamentary work, an exclusive condition that is inherent to the nature of our functions. As a member of Parliament I can give an example picked out of many. I am talking about a young MP who had just set up a legal office in his or her home town, hired staff, established social contacts, gotten involved in his community, cared for people, went into debt to start his business and build up his practice, kept up to date on the law and is aware of every change in the existing laws in order to give good service to his clients and who suddenly, because he has been a success for ten years as a lawyer or for that matter as a doctor, engineer, notary, or member of any other profession, and has built a reputation for himself through hard work and made many friends, is asked to serve in the national or parliamentary legislative assembly to take care of the interests of the public instead of just his own patients or clients. He then has to make a big sacrifice and come to Ottawa, only to find out that as a member of Parliament he has not only to take good care of his riding but also to live in Ottawa, to pass new laws, sit on committees and in the House of Commons, work as a legislator and meet with lobby groups and try to have the legislation reflect the popular will. It is a full-time job. In order to do this, he has to find someone to look after his business or office, but he is still requested to run.
Yet we all have generously accepted this call to serve our country. A number of us in so doing suffer a great financial loss. As I was saying a moment ago, nobody comes here expecting to get rich, but we do not want to get broke either if, and after serving five, six, seven, eight, ten or fifteen years, the hazards of politics cause us to be defeated or if our health gives in because our obligations as a public man or woman are so taxing that we are no longer able to travel regularly between Ottawa and our riding to fulfil our responsibilities ably and conscientiously. If at that stage we are forced out of public life because of ill health or election defeat, we find ourselves with nothing to fall back on.
I was giving the example of a professional. He no longer had an office because he had to sell it, then he had to pay tax on it because he could not incorporate. His loss was substantial. Now he has to start from scratch after an absence of 8, 10, 15 or 20 years. He has to begin anew, to get new clients, to update his knowledge, whether it be in law, medicine, or engineering or whatever, and this is not the same situation as those in private enterprise experience when they lose a job in a
Senate and House of Commons Act community, they look for another one for a few months to finally get one in the same community. They can do it much more easily that we can ourselves.
Therefore it is important to mention publicly those particularities of parliamentary life. This is true for professionals, tradesmen, for those in the field of education and it is true also for former public servants, because as soon as you get involved in politics, it is not easy to try to get back into the Public Service. More often than not, it is not an asset, it is a liability. That should not be the case but it is. Some will argue that the sacrifice men and women make to come here was their choice. However, you will agree also that if you want to serve your country, we must have the opportunity to do so not for the purpose of making money, but not to go broke either. This opportunity should not be the privilege of the rich only but should be given to the little man, either lawyer, notary, tradesman, teacher, to all those with a low or medium income, those with a very average social status.
This is the justification, Mr. Speaker, for the difference in the pension plan for members of Parliament as opposed to the private sector. We talk about being eligible to receive 75 per cent of the salary after 15 years instead of 25. I know they have such a plan in Quebec, and I am even told that it is after eight years or at any rate it is less than 15 years.

It is eight years. I am told it is 15 years in other legislatures. That seems to be the norm in legislatures where one serves one's country as an elected representative. The reason for that is that the members of Parliament are in a very special situation in that if defeated, or if they retire from public life for health or some other reason, it is extremely difficult for them to maintain the standard of living they enjoyed at the time of their retirement from politics 10 or 15 years earlier when they worked in the private sector. And I think that nobody wants such injustice in Canada. Furthermore, I am convinced that if we did not bring in these amendments to entitle members of Parliament to a pension after 15 years, we would deter responsible people from going into politics and serving in this place.
Many people, it happens at each election, refuse to leave their business or to quit their job to enter public life, not only because the salary is extremely low compared to what it should be, according to reports made to us. That is not the main reason, but they refuse because they are afraid, and rightly so, of the insecurity in store for them. Regardless of family and health problems, strictly from a personal point of view, anyone who decides to enter public life and makes a decision which brings him insecurity and uncertainty all the time he is in politics very often for the rest of his life. Because, as I said earlier, none of us enjoys job security, none of us can be sure of being re-elected, none of us can be assured that for 20, 25 years, he will be able to set aside enough money to provide

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act himself with a decent pension fund on which to live if he were handicapped or unable to return to his previous job if he does not have the money required.
Mr. Speaker, in closing on this subject let me add that a pension is not exactly an outright gift because members of Parliament will be paying for theirs. They will contribute 10 per cent of their salary each year towards it. For purposes of clarification and for the benefit of those who write about us and those who would be tempted to depreciate what we are doing, I would say that on the average a member of Parliament will serve for less than six years, and to be eligible for pension, one has to serve a minimum of six years. Therefore theoretically, nobody is entitled to the pension.
It is a fact that a rare few sit for twenty five years, and that a few more, not too many, sit for fifteen years. Not many sit for ten years, but the greatest number, the vast majority, sit less than ten years. And as I have just mentioned, those who serve an average length of time do not qualify for a pension; the average stay in Parliament is less than six years. Therefore, from the point of view of the cost to the Treasury, considering the 10 per cent contribution that we are going to make, considering what we will pay and the number of those who will in fact qualify, judging from past experience the cost to the government, to the taxpayer, will be negligible, practically nil. This is something which should be emphasized and publicized because this is not a gift that members of Parliament are offering themselves, Mr. Speaker, it is the very basic minimum a person will accept to enter public life and to serve conscientiously and without anxiety his constituents as fairly and as objectively as possible, without fear of finding himself one day in the poor house and in poor health and without any decent pension. Therefore this is the main justification for our pension system. This proposed pension plan is already applied elsewhere, sometimes much more generously, but in fact very few members will benefit from it.
I might tell you that there are now in Canada about 133, take or leave two or three, persons receiving a parliamentary pension, the overwhelming majority of them receiving a pension of less that $5,000 a year. The highest pension now received by a former parliamentarian amounts to about $17,000. I am referring to federal politicians. Some would argue that on the provincial level some former MLAs get more, but I am referring to the federal level. The highest pension now being paid in Canada amounts to about $17,000. There are only about 133 persons on pension, and most of them receive less than $5,000 a year. It is therefore an inequity, a blatant injustice, and I am glad to see that the majority of NDP members, the majority of Conservative members and the majority of Liberal members have accepted once and for all to lay aside any partisanship and endorse with such spontaneity a piece of legislation long overdue which was recommended in an independent report published and tabled by myself in the House last December. In conclusion, I would
say that a bill of this nature, a bill that concerns each and every parliamentarian, should not be drafted according to ordinary rules. It is essential, under similar circumstances, that members be consulted, which was done, as I pointed out, and it is essential too that their views be taken into consideration; this too was done as well. Again, I appreciate the sustained support of my colleagues, the House leaders, in the past several weeks, I should say the past several months, to ensure that all members were consulted. As a result of our joint efforts, a large majority of members of all parties have endorsed the provisions of this bill and I hope they will come out openly and frankly for it this evening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying how much I appreciate the review made by the President of the Privy Council and the government House leader (Mr. Pinard) of the sections and the principles of the bill. I will be speaking with respect to some parts of the bill, but not to the same extent in view of the government House leader's statement. He has saved me the trouble of quoting various opinions from the article to which he referred. These were opinions on the level of members' salaries and allowances expressed by labour leaders, business leaders, professional people and leaders. As a parliamentarian I read the article with a sense of gratefulness that there was some recognition of our work outside of this House, which is important.
I am pleased to speak on behalf of my party in favour of an increase in the indemnity for members of Parliament. I believe the increase to be fair and reasonable in the bill presented by the President of the Privy Council but I want to put it in this context, that no member in this House asks for anything more on his behalf than what the job is worth. We all ask on behalf of this institution the salary level needed to continue to attract and keep people with the skills and ideas required to make this institution function as it should. I doubt whether there is any other group of Canadians who make as many sacrifices to occupy a job than those who offer themselves as candidates to the federal House of Commons.
1 want to defend as energetically as I can the pay bill that is before us, and deal with the arguments put forward by those who say that whatever MPs are paid is too much.
Most of us are here because we want to be here. I say most because a few of my colleagues representing all sides of the House are heard to mutter from time to time after a hard day that they must have been crazy to run in the first place. But that goes with the territory and usually the next morning they feel a little better. MPs go to a lot of trouble to build a political reputation which leads to nomination and then a campaign fight which brings them here. We all like politics. We followed politics before becoming full-time politicians.
I wonder how many of us would be here if we had come across a job description for an MP in the career section of a
July 9, 1981

national newspaper. I suggest that the description would be intriguing but not very attractive. It might read this way:
Wanted: Person to act as member of Parliament. This exciting, management, professional, scientific, accounting, public service, public relations, clerical position offers endless challenge. You will represent 75,000 to 100,000 or more Canadians who have the right to phone you up at any hour of the day or night, criticize your performance on the job, fairly or unfairly, and write letters asking that you intervene with the Prime Minister or any minister on their behalf. You will be flown every week to Ottawa, which is a lovely city, except in July. While you are there you will put in a 70-hour week talking, arguing, reading and, wondering where it is getting you or anyone else. You will attend meetings from 8:30 in the morning to 11:30 at night. When you return to your riding you will be able to say hello to your spouse, if you are married, and to your children, if you have any, before departing to your constituency office, riding functions and more meetings. Fully rested, you will fly out Sunday night for another week in Ottawa. If you work hard, take chances, stay out of trouble and get lucky, you might end up as a cabinet minister, or even worse. Pay: $32,700 per annum, falling further behind inflation every year. The successful candidate must have extensive personal savings or be single.
Most people reading that ad might consider $32,700 a little low for the skills demanded and the workload expected.
But I want to say that the job of a member of Parliament can be challenging. Being an MP can be worthwhile, which is why most of us came here. The job can be absorbing, which is why most of us stay. In the long run it can be exhausting, discouraging and fruitless, which is why many leave. For the last two decades it has been what it was not previously, and that is a full-time occupation.
For the last four or five years, MPs have been badly underpaid. For many members of this House the frustrations of parliamentary life have been compounded by the rising anxiety over family finances. That is a matter which this House must face.
The House of Commons does not exist to offer monetary rewards for those who may come here on the make. Equally, it should not penalize those who come to the House at the peak of their careers when their energy and stamina are at their greatest. The salary level should, in fact, be a neutral factor. It should not be high enough to constitute the principal attraction to the job, but equally not so low that it is the main deterrent against running for Parliament or staying here. The job should be accessible to any Canadian who feels he has something to offer, whether married or single, old or young, rich or poor, with or without children, male or female. As is often said, this is supposed to be a representative institution and a low salary level should not act as an unintended social filter to those who would like to come here. That is the purpose, as I see it, of this bill.
The important question that we and the country have to face is quite simply, how much is the job worth? Mclsaac and Balcer based their proposal for a salary level of $45,000 per year on a comparison of MPs' jobs with others requiring similar skills. I do not think there are others demanding similar hours. Mclsaac and Balcer looked principally at comparable bureaucratic salary levels, which are substantially below those of the private sector since, in a bureaucracy, it is difficult to measure performance. That difficulty applies to ourselves as well as MPs.
Senate and House of Commons Act
Having made that comparison, the Mclsaac and Balcer report called for a minimum salary of $45,000 per annum to be reached in four increments of $3,600, with an annual adjustment based on the findings of the Pay Research Bureau on the average salary changes for supervisory, managerial and professional employees.
Most of us in this House thought that that was a fair approach. We hoped it would solve both the immediate and the long-range problems. We all wish that we had a boss we could go to on an individual basis and argue the merits of our own case, as we would if we were in the private sector or if we belonged to a union or employee association where we could go as a group. We would rather have almost any other arrangement than the one we have now.
We support the adoption of a fair salary level and a formula to more or less maintain it. I will come to the "more or less" in a moment.
What we have in the bill before us is substantially less than the minimum recomended by Mclsaac and Balcer. However, we can accept the importance of a package which can be accepted by everyone as representing a substantial majority of the three parties in this House. Instead of $45,000, it will be $40,200 effective July 1, 1980 with the first cost of living increase coming in January 1, 1981. As a yearly increased index, instead of the Pay Research Bureau reports as recommended by Mclsaac-Balcer, it will be the lesser of the consumer price index or industrial composite, minus 1 per cent of that lesser figure. The expense allowance will remain as it is now, instead of being divided into an expense allowance and housing allowance, as recommended by Mclsaac-Balcer.
I know that certain segments of the country of the country will soon emerge-I hope they won't but they will-in full cry against this reduced figure, even though it is well below what many of us in the House could make elsewhere and well below that of most of the people we deal with daily in the Ottawa bureaucracy and as representatives of the private sector. Nevertheless, the suggestions made in this bill go some way to correcting the imbalance. On behalf of my party, we accept it.
I believe the new salary level is within the range of what the job is worth, if perhaps at the low end of the scale. I also know that a great many arguments are made against any raises at all which have nothing to do with a fair salary level. I wish to deal with them in the next few moments because I do not believe that those arguments which are raised are as unanswerable as their proponents would have everyone believe.
One argument which is more often alluded to than openly avowed is the one I call "for the honour" argument. This line of reasoning suggests there should be a measure of sacrifice in the job of being a member of Parliament and that it is somehow unworthy to ask for a raise in pay in the same manner as anyone else would. The suggestion is that an MP lacks patriotism in expressing dissatisfaction with the pay that exists.

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act
I believe that this argument mistakes the nature of the sacrifice an MP already makes. It ignores the changes in the conditions of employment over the past two decades, and in the bargain it argues that a family can be fed with honour. Even if an MP's pay were doubled, it could be argued effectively that an MP puts up with long hours, tedious travel and family separation which would drive people in the private sector either to premature ulcers or premature retirement. There are very real sacrifices undertaken willingly in the line of public duty. If anything, they are more tangible than the monetary penalties which can be staved off by dipping into savings, if one has then, or by regarding the position of an MP as a temporary venture.
In previous eras, going back to confederation, the job of the MP was perhaps more prestigious than it is now. It was undertaken mostly by people who, when they came to the House, where older than the member today. They were already leaders in their communities before coming here. Many had substantial wealth and did not need a salary. For those not in the fortunate position, the sacrifice was marginal since Parliament sat only a few months, often at a time when there was little to be done on the farm or when the business or professional office could be run by associates for a short period of time. The sacrifice, such as it was, was made by those who had a great deal to sacrifice.
Today parliamentary business is a full-time occupation. All of us frown on those who try to take the money as a parliamentarian and then go out and attempt to make more money somewhere else. We look upon this as a full-time occupation. The reason we frown on it is because that kind of member, and there are a few, is not here when he is needed. He cannot be counted on. We here and the public generally have to come to regard this job, quite rightly, as a full-time occupation.
Those in this House who do not need their parliamentary salary are in a minority. Needless to say, those people are not asking for this raise except in recognition of the position of their colleagues. Increasingly, MPs who come here are exactly the type that the public clamours for: young, energetic people, representatives of the bulk of the population, both men and women.
More and more of our MPs are young or middle-aged. More and more have growing families. They do not expect the people of Canada to give them the kind of incomes they could have expected had they continued in private life. They do ask people to understand that a young family cannot be raised on the honour of having a parent as an MP. The expense and the natural strain of raising a family are increased, not diminished, by constant separation, a duplication of residences and the stress of political life.
Another frequent argument against a raise for MPs is that they should set an example in the fight against inflation. Aside from the point I just made, that MPs increasingly are subject to the same or more serious pressures as anyone else, I would argue that parliamentarians have already made significant sacrifices in the inflationary fight. Even with this raise and the yearly increases, as was put by the President of the Privy
Council (Mr. Pinard), we have not seen the last debate in this House dealing with the way in which MPs' pay has fallen behind. I ask my friends to mark those words.
In 1975 the salary level was made retroactive to 1974 and set at $24,000. It was to be increased in each year, beginning January 1, 1976, by the amount of increase in the industrial composite index or 7 per cent, whichever was the lesser. The 1976 escalation was cancelled by this House so that the salary level was frozen at the same level for 1974, 1975 and 1976. How many groups in the economy can point to a total voluntary freeze for three years?
The 1976 freeze cost members of Parliament not only for that year but also for every successive year, since the base upon which escalation would take off thereafter was smaller for each subsequent escalation. The present salary is $32,700. If we had increased it by only 7 per cent each year-and neither the industrial composite index nor the consumer price index registered that low in that period of time-we would now be at $36,336.
Some people-and I suggest there are a number-accuse us of trying to keep up with inflation. If our salary had kept up with the consumer price index, it would now be approximately $40,000. If it had kept up with the industrial composite index, it would now be almost $43,000 and the expense allowance would be even higher. As Mclsaac-Balcer showed, if it had kept its position relative to comparable professional or managerial jobs, it would be higher still. Throughout this period of escalation when the escalations were running behind, the job of the member of Parliament became more demanding, the hours longer and the sessions more dragged out, as this one is dragging out. Compared with any measure of inflation we lost ground in terms of salary every year. Both the cumulative total loss and the loss in salary position has been substantial. I have to ask myself a question: How many of those critics, however well-intentioned they may be, have made similar sacrifices over the past seven years.
The new salary level puts us roughly at where we would have been, but of course it does not take into account the accumulated loss on the escalation, the loss which has forced many members to dip into their savings and into other resources. The new formula refers to the lower of the consumer price index or the industrial composite minus 1 per cent. That is obviously a better arrangement from our point of view, but the 1 per cent will accumulate-this is what I meant earlier when I said "Mark my words"-and after 10 or 12 years this time, instead of seven, we will find that we have fallen seriously behind. How many other groups in the economy have accepted a wage package which locks them into a salary scale which guarantees now that in a decade they will be 10 per cent to 15 per cent behind then current salary levels?
But some say as an answer: "It is your own fault as a member of Parliament that inflation has risen and will rise so much. You promised to fix inflation, and you did not. You do not deserve a raise for failing." Let us leave aside in answering
July 9, 1981

that attack the fact that very few of us promised our constituents we could stop inflation. Let us leave aside the complex factors causing inflation and the myriad of cures which have been advanced for ending it. Let us just look at our system of government and the party system which animates it.
We are not elected as individuals to solve Canada's problems individually. As much as we all hope we are the ones to have to cure revealed to us, that is not our lot. We come in large part as party politicians supporting a party platform. Those opposite me now support an anti-inflation program put forward by the executive which consists of most of the ladies and gentlemen in the two front rows. They as a government have made their choices and, with luck, the people of Canada will hold them responsible as a government for the failure of their policies. When we are in office, we would be held responsible for our policies. That is how the system works. It is wrong in practice and ludicrous in theory to put members of Parliament individually on a commission basis and say, "Your pay is frozen until you cure inflation." Members of Parliament should be paid for the job they are constitutionally called upon to do, which is either to defend the government on the one hand, or to oppose it on the other and propose an alternative. That is our job.
Another line is to say that members of Parliament want a raise to attract better people. There must be an admission that they themselves leave a lot to be desired. I think we recognize the qualities of the people most responsible for making this Parliament run and we wish there were more of them. We know the demands put on people who finally reach the cabinet. Some of us have been there and we hope more people with the necessary qualities reach Parliament. To be honest, we all count ourselves as the sort of people we should be attracting. We all have our own nominees for colleagues who could be replaced for the benefit of this institution. That is not really the point any more. Parliament has been successful in interesting more and more qualified people in running, and the raise in pay and benefits which has paralleled the increase in demands made has been one of those factors. This does not apply simply to the increased number who have left the recognized professions such as medicine, law, business or teaching, but also to the larger number of non-professional people who have established themselves as strong leaders in their communities or strong leaders in their unions and who felt a parliamentary career was a logical next step. The real point is that once we get them here we must keep them- within the bounds, of course, of party competition.
It does us relatively little good if we get better and better people who spend less and less time here in the work of this Parliament. There are already enough non-salary incentives to leave, but a discussion of these belongs in a debate on parliamentary reform. It takes time to reach maximum effectiveness as a parliamentarian. As a Parliament and as a country we cannot afford to have most of our promising new recruits leave in disgust after one term of financial sacrifice or political frustration. We can do something about the former now and
Senate and House of Commons Act perhaps about the latter when my friend, the President of the Privy Council, brings in his reform package in the fall.
There is another argument, and the argument goes this way: Members knew what they were getting into, so why do they not just get on with it? That applies to both salaries and conditions. I really have to ask myself how many employees in this country would accept the argument that, because they wanted the job they were in and knew roughly what the salary and the conditions were, they have no right to ask for a change if a case can be made. If anyone suggested that to a union leader in this country, he would be subjected to a string of epithets of which "reactionary" would be the mildest. I doubt that many really did know what the job would entail, but that is another story.
We run as members of Parliament because we want to do things for our country, not because we tacitly accept that everything about the job is perfect. Certainly there will never be a shortage of candidates, but so what? It is just as important for the health of our democracy to ensure that the candidates are qualified and will try to earn the right to stay in the House as to ensure an unlimited supply.
We are told that it is not reasonable to count only our salary and that we should count our allowances as well. In fact, we are told, since the allowance is not taxed we should count it at more than its face value. Members who are struggling to make ends meet at just over $30,000 are finding sources outside quoting their salaries at figures such as $50,000. It is a specious figure and reflects poorly on those who use it.
Members of Parliament have a wide range of expenses, including the tax-free one, because they are needed to do the job. The most obvious expense is maintaining two homes, but to the cost of housing can be added the cost of family separation, the cost of having almost no leisure time for do-it-yourselfing, the ceaseless demands for donations, dinner tickets and the incidentals of constant travel and public appearances. Sure, some members may make a bit on the expense allowance. Lots of others, however, dip into their savings or investments to subsidize their position as an MP.
The allowance of $14,000-$14,400 as of today-is a compromise which has been traditionally supported by all parties. It is for expenses, and for the great majority of members of Parliament it is necessary for expenses. If an executive officer or an employee of the public service or any business was sent to Vancouver in the course of his work, his travel expenses would be paid. This job calls us from Vancouver and elsewhere to Ottawa.
A final argument holds that if we wish to use as an argument the salary we can make outside this House, we should work outside the House. Well, there are two replies to that argument. The one I have already made is the fact that we wish that a more realistic salary does not in any way diminish our sense of public duty in being here. It simply means that we are not monks or janissaries; rather we are ordinary men and women with ordinary requirements. Second,

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act
no one is asking for the money he might have made elsewhere. A substantial number of members gave up high salaries from a sense of duty. They did not and do not expect to attain the same earning levels as they had before they became members of Parliament. They do not ask that the indemnity be lavish, merely that it not be derisory. This is the situation we are in if this bill is not passed.
There is only one valid argument, Mr. Speaker, in assessing the salary levels: What is fair for the job to be done? That is an argument put in this House of Commons, in the legislatures across the country, but it is more fairly and honestly put and recognized in every job occupation outside this place. What is fair for the job to be done? The political process can only be harmed if we try and take legislators and say they must be the whipping boys or must set an example beyond what is reasonable. All the arguments I have referred to sound impressive unless you stop to think about their implications, if followed through, the best people would be discouraged from coming to the House, and those here would seek ways to leave if we do not address the problem now.
In every occupation the salary level speaks for the employer in expressing the regard he has for his employees and the extent to which he values their services. It speaks to the question of what the job is worth in every occupation. A low salary, permanently held low, would serve to devalue this institution and we could not expect it to attract the people who should be here.
As MPs we are targets, but that does not mean we have to sit meekly in the face of some of the nonsense and hypocrisy that is from time to time hurled in our direction. I would have been happy to have had the opportunity to defend the salary proposals put forward in the Mclsaac-Balcer report. The salary set there was a defensible and appropriate one, reached after great consideration by some people who know. Having said that, I have even less hesitation in speaking in support of the proposal of the government, which is considerably lower.
Now, before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the pension proposal in this bill. It would raise our contribution from 7 per cent to 10 per cent of salary, with an additional 1 per cent for later indexing, and another 1 per cent for a surviving spouse provision.
We support this provision for several reasons, including the assurances given us by the government about the finances of the fund. That assurance has been extremely important in our minds and in our decision to accept the proposals. There have been criticisms about the pension arrangements for MPs. However, I put in to the House that this new scheme is not a departure in principle from what has gone on before. It is a straightforward exchange of higher contributions for higher benefits. Under this scheme the maximum benefit level is reached after 15 years, when it is 75 per cent of the six best years. It should be noted this refers only to salaries. The allowances and so on do not enter into this consideration at all. I make that point so that we do not get the same distortion on that coupling as could occur if it were done with respect to pensions.
I think more people are familiar with the rationale for a pension scheme for members of Parliament. Many of the arguments against the pension are made against what might be called the "worst cases". Whenever an argument is made against the pension plan for MPs, it is always the worst case that could possibly be picked, ignoring the fact that for most members the provisions are reasonable and in fact the actual payment levels are really quite low.
Most MPs come into the House over the age of 35 or 40. A 15-year chunk out of their career at this point, with very little extra salary to contribute to an RRSP, means that the prime contributing years have been removed. Not many people could leave the House and re-enter the employment market at 50 or 55, and in the next decade or so not only re-establish themselves in an interrupted career, but make an adequate provision for 20 or more years of retirement. That is the reason the plan was conceived in the first place, and for the way it was conceived.
Similarly, someone who only meets the minimum qualification of six years and gets a small pension entitlement is not being pensioned for life but is simply receiving a proportionate contribution to their eventual retirement plan. You have only to look at the levels that are paid after six years of service as a member of Parliament. Perhaps when we reach the stage as a country of complete pension portability, none of this would be necessary. However, we have not yet reached that point.
There is an impression that former members are already receiving luscious pensions and I would like to repeat some of the figures mentioned in the Mclsaac-Balcer report, which were in term taken from the annual report on the administration of the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act for 1978-79. There were 218 MPs receiving pensions along with 34 surviving spouses and one dependant child. Of the MPs, one received between $21,000 and $21,999; one received between $20,000 and $20,999; and one received between $19,000 and $19,999. Altogether, 24 received more than $10,000 and 144 received less than $5,000 a year. That is not a picture of a pension scheme run wild. Given the assurances of the soundness of the increased deduction and benefit levels, I do not believe there should be any problem in the future. However, that is something this Parliament has a duty to watch, review and monitor constantly. The situation of MPs is different from others in the economy, and the pension plan for which they pay a high rate reflects that difference.
I believe this bill is supported by almost all hon. members of the House. It does not have this support because a theoretical figure has been plucked out of the air to be embraced and held to the bosoms of a group of rapacious members of Parliament. It is supported because members of Parliament know by their own day-to-day experience and that of their colleagues that the present pay level is far too low to meet the expenses encountered, to compensate for the skills which are required, and to encourage the interest in a parliamentary career needed
July 9, 1981

to maintain the effectiveness of this institution. This is why the bill is before us.
I want to close by saying that the overwhelming majority of my party and I support the proposals in this bill. For that reason we agreed earlier today to the order of the House which would allow this matter to be considered.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
I believe the position taken by my colleagues in the House of Commons and I is a responsible one. Like most other occupations, members of Parliament face the ravishes of inflation. Members of Parliament have children in schools and colleges. Members of Parliament have to renew mortgages at 20 per cent interest rates. They pay taxes too and purchase automobiles which today cost about as much as a house cost when I first bought a home. Some members require two homes because of the distance they live from Ottawa. If they are unlucky, this means two 20 per cent mortgages.
My party and I do not support the total package as presented in the Balcer-Mclsaac report because we feel it was too rich a proposal in a number of ways. Balcer-Mclsaac called for a
Senate and House of Commons Act
$3,600 per year increase over four years. My party rejected this. Balcer-Mclsaac called for a $500 accommodation allowance, but this was rejected as well on the ground that members of Parliament already enjoy a tax-free, non-accountable expense allowance. Therefore, we believe we should pay our rent out of what I would describe as this adequate tax-free portion.
While I am certain that we will not be thanked for it, either by some of my own colleagues, some members of the other parties or some members of the general public who think that any raise for MPs by any definition is too much, I believe it is a responsible act to scale down the recommendations of Balcer-Mclsaac by one third or approximately $5,000 envisioned in the fourth year of their report and one third across the board along the same lines.
There will be some who claim that this is a bad time to have a pay hike, that this is a bad time to discuss a pay increase or the benefit package of members of Parliament. Of those who claim this I should like to ask: When is a good time? There are no good times; there are only bad times as far as some are concerned.
I was here in 1970 when salaries were readjusted and, except for one New Democratic Party member of Parliament, my party opposed the pay raise then. Again in 1974, which was the last time the salaries of members of Parliament were revised, my party, except for three of its members, again opposed the pay bill. It is in our tradition to oppose pay raises, especially if we consider them to be unreasonable.
Some of the newer members in all corners of the House should realize that if my party had been successful in blocking the pay hikes of 1970 and 1974, members would still be earning what they were earning when I came here in 1968. For those members who might not remember, it was the staggering sum of $12,000 taxable salary, supported by a $6,000 tax-free allowance.
Some people would argue that being a member of Parliament is a calling somewhat like the ministry and that we should all be prepared to accept the long hours, the travel, the weekends packed full of meetings and public appearances, the resulting family tensions to which others have referred and so forth, as part of our sacrifice for having the privilege of serving the people of Canada.
Members of my caucus do not accept the argument, however, that high pay is the single most important criterion for attracting so-called good men and women to Parliament. We know that there are hundreds of good men and women serving communities all across Canada who are not particularly highly paid, so we totally reject this "attract good men and women" argument. No one goes into politics to get rich, but it is equally true that members of Parliament are not poor compared with the rest of the country. Speaking for my party, we do not expect to earn what doctors earn, what top deputy ministers earn at $85,000 to $91,000 in government ministries, or even what hockey players earn at $100,000 per year on the average. But we think it is irresponsible to encourage MPs to take home a salary which is less by $5,000 than that of an

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act
elementary school principal in my riding or roughly equivalent to that of an interior IWA tradesman in my province if we add a bit of overtime. This is not said to demean in any way either the elementary school principal or the tradesman. And surely the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), whatever we might think of him, is worth at least somewhere near the financial reward earned by the average NHL hockey player.
Since 1974 members of Parliament have averaged a 4.4 per cent increase in their indemnities, while the consumer price index climbed 68 per cent by 1980 and the industrial composite jumped 78.2 per cent by the same year. Essentially the salary proposal before us does little more than catch up to where MPs were in 1974. That fact in itself makes the package worthy of serious consideration. Other people as disparate as John Bulloch of the Federation of Independent Business, former British Columbia Supreme Court judge J. V. Clyne and Dennis McDermott of the CLC all agree that members of Parliament need better salaries.
My friend, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen), has figured out that this package is worth about 21 per cent over 11 years, plus COLA, if spoken and defined in union terms. No one, unless he has been elected to the House of Commons at least once, has any conception of the hourly demands placed upon members of Parliament. Absolutely invisible to members of the public is the time that MPs spend on such things as party policy decisions, the hours we spend on the committee work of various kinds, such as estimates, annual reports, task forces which sit in the summer, as the alternative energy one did last summer, and as the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements task force intends to sit this summer. No one knows the time it takes to study legislation before the House. Equally invisible is the preparation of speeches, the phone calls, the letters related to constituents' problems, or for that matter, the time spent on travel to and from our constituencies. We are busy people and, I think, effective people. In the main, I think it is time the public heard that statement in complimenting MPs once in a while.
If I may be permitted a brief or perhaps even a lengthy personal note, I represent a British Columbia constituency. I go home virtually every weekend. If any listener or viewer thinks flying across Canada and back once a week is a real treat, I would like to disabuse them of that misconception.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT

speechtext:
It takes at least an hour for me to get to the airport Friday evenings, and if my plane is not late, as it usually is, we leave for Vancouver at 7:05 p.m. The plane, if it gets to Vancouver, arrives at about 9:30 p.m. Vancouver time, but that is 12:30 a.m. Ottawa time. By the time I get to my home in Mission, after driving about 60 miles-I think that is about 100 kilometres-it is two hours later. By the time I get home, it is 2:30 a.m. for me, because I remain on Ottawa time. For me, that travel is tough. But for B.C. members, like my colleagues here and some from the other parties who do not
live in the lower mainland, it is terrible. Consider for a moment the travel problems confronting the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) or the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), or the Okanagan and Vancouver Island members.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
