speechtext: Try Newfoundland!

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
These individuals must catch local connecting flights later on that evening after they reach Vancouver or spend the night in Vancouver as a stopover before completing their journey or their trip home. These members like to get home and keep in touch with their constituents too, but the vast size of Canada makes that extremely difficult. The travel time and the expenditure of energy in such travel is immense, and I do not think very many people realize that.
Of course, there will be people who will say that if the work is so tough and the travel is so rough, why does one run in the first place? I think that is a reasonable question, and it is a good question. However, I think it begs the real question whether our salaries are falling behind the cost of living or not; and it also ignores the hours members of Parliament spend on travel, as well as time they spend on their jobs in Ottawa and their jobs in their constituencies, whether it is on weekends or in the summertime. There is seldom a weekend I do not attend some public function in my own riding.
So all in all, in discussing the matter with other MPs, we find that it is a rare week when most MPs do not work from perhaps 9 a.m. in the morning to 10 p.m. in the evening. If one multiplies that by about six days, the total amounts to roughly between 75 and 80 hours per week. That is the number of hours at straight time, say at $12 an hour. I am not talking about overtime, time and a half, or double time. Incidentally, an interior tradesman in the IWA in my province has just received an offer of $16.95 an hour. This is what a tradesman can receive. However, if one multiplies 75 or 80 hours by $12 per hour, one cannot get very far away from $1,000 a week. If one says $1,000 a week, one has to say that amounts to roughly $12,000 per year more than what we are asking for in this package.
Some of us might wonder again why someone like me would speak in favour of this legislation, given my traditions. Unfortunately, we seem over the years to have been saying two rather contradictory things. On the one hand, we have said that since we do not want Parliament to become the exclusive preserve of the privileged classes and the wealthy, we support decent salaries, pensions and benefits to enable even those of modest means to stand for public office without undue sacrifice to themselves or their families. On the other hand, our voting record indicates that we do not really believe this at all, and we have acted over the years to keep salaries relatively low. I think we have been responsible historically. The result of this action, nevertheless, has meant that at least some able people of all political persuasions have been discouraged from seeking public office because their personal financial responsibilities preclude them from standing for Parliament. I think that is a fact.
July 9, 1981

It is probably true that I personally, as an individual, would not be unduly damaged if there were no revision of our salaries, other than the benefits which would come about under the normal course of the 7 per cent. However, I believe that the position of the MP deserves to be recognized, and the position of the MP as related to salary paid to the office, cannot fall behind unduly. 1 have no children at home any more, personally. My obligations to my wife and family are not nearly as great as they once were. If Parliament granted no increase beyond the 7 per cent annual increase, I personally would not feel persecuted financially.
However, I remember with great clarity how things were in 1968 when I was first elected. My first term was in 1968-1969.
I took home $12,000 taxable and $6,000 non-taxable. I was paying on a house in Coquitlam, where my wife remained. I had one child in junior high school. I had two others in two different universities, and I was so broke that I could afford no apartment. Never mind the accommodation allowance; I recall sleeping in a room with a couple of other members of Parliament.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext: Move into a tenement.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
Well, I would not want my plight to sound too bad! However, I will say this. I certainly had no automobile in Ottawa. A second automobile for use in Ottawa was naturally out of the question.
The following year we sold our house in Coquitlam so we could afford to buy something here, and we moved to Ottawa. I brought one wife, one child and one car. We all moved to Ottawa. I do not mean to be funny about this; I do not think it is funny. I do not want anyone to weep too much, but I do not think it is funny, either.
Our move to Ottawa, of course, meant that I no longer had a home in my riding. Therefore, each time I visited I had to rent a car and maybe sleep at my mother's house or crash the home of some political supporter. I do not want hon. members to weep over this. I got by. I am still here. I was defeated but later I was re-elected. The shock to my system was not that great. I got by and so did my family. I had to give up my UBC pension for six years, because becoming an MP meant I would have to pick up both the university's portion plus my own and I could not afford the cost.
I was first elected in 1968. I was out for five years. Therefore, I can anticipate a proportionally minimal retirement allowance, based on four years of low salary when I first came here, if and when I am next defeated or retire.
Again, I say I will get by; but it can be argued that Parliament is no longer the private preserve of the wealthy, neither is it any longer the private preserve of the elderly. There are now dozens of young MPs here with growing families who intend to make a career out of politics. For them, serving in Parliament is far more than a calling; it is a career with rather risky job security provisions.
Senate and House of Commons Act
These young members need decent salaries, decent pensions and decent severance pay once they are defeated-as they surely will be. Since 1968, 218 members have failed to win election. I believe the average term of an MP is less than six years. If their terms are less it means that most MPs fail to qualify for even the minimum pension. They will not qualify under this bill either, so I repeat, this package is not overly generous. It is both reasonable and responsible. Even if some of the more senior MPs do not need more money, some of the younger ones with families need the improvements badly. On behalf of this party, I support the recommendations contained in the bill.
Let me speak briefly now about severance pay, and again I call upon my own experiences to illustrate the need for some form of severance pay for those MPs who are defeated, as most are, before they qualify for a minimum pension after six years.
I was defeated in 1974, but while serving here I was on political leave from an enlightened institution called the University of British Columbia and I still am. The day after I was defeated in 1974 I went back on staff at UBC, so the lack of severance pay was not an issue for me. I had security and I had tenure, but hundreds of others do not. The readjustment to "civvy street" is much more difficult for them.
My four NDP colleagues who went down to defeat in 1980 were not so lucky. Three of the four had seven distinguished years as parliamentarians. All were good MPs, but as so often happens when vote shifts occur, being a good MP is like being a spectator at a shoot-out. You can be gunned down anyway. Of the four, not one had a job to go back to the day after the election. One though, after some months, was reluctantly taken back by his school district because the contract demanded it. Two others still cannot find jobs equal to those they left on first becoming elected and the third started his own business and is in debt to the bank for thousands of dollars.
I have said nothing about lost promotional opportunities in the prime of one's career life. I have not spoken of catching up professionally after an extended absence from a job or profession. After an absence of six years, I felt I did not know the literature; I was dated, and it took a long time to get back where I was professionally when I left. I do not mean financially because I was covered financially. I have not spoken either of housing and domestic factors that make the readjustment of a defeated MP extremely difficult.
I think, tough, I have said enough to make a fairly convincing case for severance pay for defeated MPs, and I think I can say, despite our differences on certain parts in the bill and its benefits, that this party agrees that severance pay is essential and supports it 100 per cent.
Now let me turn to pensions. Many people think that upon retirement or defeat all MPs receive pensions bountiful enough to enable them to take numerous world tours, dine only in the finest restaurants and stay at the best-hotels. From the laugh-

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act
ter, I notice that some hon. members are not convinced; but most of the general public believes that.
As I have already stated, most MPs do not receive any pension whatsoever because they are not here long enough to qualify. If you do not believe me, just ask some of those nine-month MPs who came and went with the Clark government. How many? Too many, say the Tories.
As the Balcer-Mclsaac report points out, in 1979 there was a grand total of 218 former MPs receiving pensions. Of these, 101, or virtually half, receive pensions less than $3,000, which is lower than the basic old age pension today. There will be no world tours for these pensioners.
The next highest group includes 93 former MPs and they receive between $3,000 and $10,000 per year. This is not lavish when one considers that a pensioner on old age security and with the guaranteed income supplement today receive $5,160 per year. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is known far and wide for his achievements on behalf of the pensioners of Canada. I am not saying that our elderly receive too much. I am saying that if you put it in the proper perspective, the 93 former MPs who receive pensions of between $3,000 and $10,000 per year paid their share of their premium. It was not a gift.
Our present pension requires a 7.5 per cent premium to be paid and the one we are considering will require a 10 per cent premium at the minimum. As was pointed out earlier, the indexing portion will cost another 1 per cent and if one wants a decent spouse's allowance for a survivor, the premium will cost an additional 1 per cent. The contribution, therefore, is between 10 per cent and 12 per cent annually.
This is a pension to which MPs will contribute probably more than the government's share. It is no gift. It is a pension like any other pension and takes 15 years to mature. How many members of Parliament last for 15 years? Very few.
I spoke on this subject of the pension ten or 11 years ago, Mr. Speaker. At that time I believed that no one should be eligible for a pension under the age of 55. In fact, I regret that this bill does not include this provision. When we last discussed pensions I was 46, and I moved a motion to that effect. Of course, it was defeated. I cannot move that motion today since I would hardly be considered objective, being past that magic age, but I would not object if another member moved such a motion. I do not want to move it because it could be considered favouring my own age group over some of the other members and their interests, so I will not do that.
I hope that this has not sounded like a litany of gripes, Mr. Speaker. As has been said earlier, this is an exciting and important place to be. People are not here just for the money, they are here for a lot of reasons. Among the most important of the reasons is the fact that they like politics, they like serving their country, they like the variety and the challenge.
I should like to pay respect and show my gratitude to the people who have sent me and my colleagues here and have given us an opportunity, which comes to very few people, to serve our country in this institution. It is an experience available only to few people and I am grateful for it. I do not want any defence of the bill to sound like I am sick of my job, therefore.
In conclusion, I am supremely aware that, as humans, we are all prone to cloak our actions in the most noble of motives, and probably I am guilty of this human foible today, I do not know. What I do know is that in 1970 I typically voted against the pay raise and later took the money. At that point I decided that, if I ever intended to take the money again, I would vote for a package if it was fair. I think this package is fair and I intend to vote for it.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing an environmental bill of rights which would, with respect to federal matters:
1.	emphasize the right of an individual or group of individuals to initiate court action when in their judgment the environment is in danger, without first having to prove that they have suffered personal or economic damage;
2.	shift the burden of proof to the polluter after the individual or group has established that damage to the environment is likely;
3.	make information held by private companies and governments on the handling, storing and treatment of hazardous products and related manufacturing processes accessible to the public, with certain exceptions to be defined in regulations;
4.	give the court the power to set interim or permanent injunctions in an action commenced under the act; and
5.	give the court the power to set standards where there are none and order a polluter to comply.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in this motion I am asking the government to introduce legislation that would protect the environmental rights of Canadians for the following reasons.
With science and technology advancing in leaps and bounds and with a life style that still encourages consumption rather than conservation, the environment is increasingly coming under attack. As citizens, we need the means to act so that we can prevent damage caused by pollution. We need this legislation because today the citizen does not have real recourse in attempting to prevent an initiative that might seriously damage his environment and even his livelihood. Usually he can only claim for damages after the fact.
We need legislation to protect environmental rights because present laws and practices have the effect of putting the citizen in a much weaker position than the industries that pollute. As described in a book entitled "Poisons in Public" by Ross Howard, an environmental journalist who wrote for the Canadian Environmental Law Research Foundation:
The polluter's use can stop the swimmer from using and enjoying a lake, but the swimmer's use cannot stop the polluter from polluting the lake ... Even in a world with rules against pollution ... the leverage inherent in resource consumers means that they can continue their conduct until sued. In short, they almost inevitably will be defendants (of the right to use and pollute) and those whose uses preserve rather than deteriorate will ineluctably be plaintiffs.

July 9, 1981
The Environment
What recourse have the people suffering from mercury poisoning in the Wabigoon River against control orders which have been delayed for a decade, or against the company that threatened to shut down rather than clean up? What recourse does the small resort owner have against the polluters causing acid rain which is slowly killing the lake on which his business depends? What recourse do the Nishga Indians, the B.C. Medical Association, the B.C. Federation of Labour, the Anglican Church and environment groups in that province have against the dumping of toxic waste into Alice Arm Inlet by the Amax Corporation?
These examples support the argument that it is no longer enough to compensate the victims of pollution. This is why preventative legislation is needed in the form of this proposal or something similar to it.
Environmental protection is not a new concept. This and past Liberal governments have taken many positive steps. There is the Environmental Contaminants Act which among other things has led to the banning of PCBs and chlorofluoro-carbons in many products. It allows for "interested parties" to initiate boards of review into regulations and I am told that "interested parties" is being interpreted widely.
Under the Clean Air Act, the public now has 60 days to comment on new regulations. The results have been positive. Mercury air emission regulations made in 1976 were strengthened considerably after public comment. This act has been amended recently to strengthen the fight against acid rain. Since 1973 review panels have been set up to ensure that environmental effects are taken into account as early as possible in federal programs, projects and activities. We have had an independent environmental advisory council since 1972 to provide the Minister of the Environment with informed advice on problems and policies respecting the Canadian environment. Encouraging developments are under way regarding the testing of toxic chemicals used in industry, and I welcome recent statements by the minister which support the advantages of pulling together into one piece of legislation the various acts which deal with environmental protection. The list could go on.
The motion today proposes another step towards ensuring a clean and healthy environment. How? By opening up the system, by encouraging public action to a much greater extent. Under present procedures citizens are not told in advance what standards of pollution control the government intends to apply to polluters. In fact, in Canada pollution control is accomplished through established standards and emission rates negotiated privately between the polluter and the regulator. Without well researched and well organized comment and analysis by public interest groups and independent experts, issues do not receive a full and fair hearing. Therefore, affected groups feel alienated. With consultation, the better the standards are likely to be, the more public support they are likely to gain.
Traditionally Canadians have relied on their governments to protect the environment and regulate industry. By encouraging public action, citizens too will have a responsibility in protecting the environment.
We are proposing that individuals or groups of individuals be given the right to initiate court action when in their judgment the environment is in danger, without first having to prove that they have suffered personal or economic damage. In essence, this right would permit a citizen to sue for a violation of environmental quality rights in much the same way that one has always been able to claim that a property or contract right has been violated.
It is important that the suit be initiated without first having to prove personal or economic damage because this can be either impossible to prove conclusively or it might be beyond the means of a private individual to produce sufficient technical evidence to support his complaint. The citizen would have to establish first that damage to the environment is likely. The burden of proof would then shift to the polluter. This is the second point in the motion. Today, under present legislation, the major burden of proving even the most basic issues, such as pollution source and impact, is on the plaintiff-in other words, the victim-in almost every lawsuit, and this is virtually an impossible task.
For example, anti-pollution action under the federal Fisheries Act often ends up in court. The onus is on the government to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that a polluting substance is "deleterious to fish". However, if sublethal effects are suggested but not confirmed, it is hard to find expert witnesses to testify. The case is therefore lost and prosecution cannot be carried out.
Under the Environmental Contaminants Act, government officials must be satisfied that a substance is or will constitute a significant danger before it can be regulated. The government must prove its suspicions before it can move in reaction to a chemical already on the market. Unfortunately, the most definitive proof is a victim.
As an aside I would like to add that the initiatives that the Canadian government has taken at the OECD to enforce on all member nations standard tests of toxic chemicals are commendable. It is unfortunate that these efforts have been "shot down" by the Americans. However, even if successful, our action would not have protected the ctitizen against any of the 50,000-I repeat, 50,000-chemicals on the market today.
The third point in the motion calls for access to information on the handling, storing and treatment of hazardous products, and it has already been addressed by Bill C-43, the access to information bill. Once it is enacted, the bill will enforce the principle that government information be available to the public and specifically provide for public access to records containing the results of product or environmental testing carried out by government institutions.
The fourth point in this motion, to give courts the power to set interim or permanent injunctions in actions commenced under the act, would have the advantage that damage or threats of damage to the environment would not continue unabated during long court cases. It supports the principle that toxic chemicals should be regarded with suspicion and "guilty
July 9, 1981

until proved innocent". This power would be similar to powers given to the courts under the Fisheries Act where the court can order a polluter to refrain from committing further offences.
The fifth and final point dealing with judicial review flows from the Michigan environmental protection act of 1970. Quite frankly, I would prefer parliamentary review on a continuous basis combined with prior public consultations, but 1 have included this point of the purpose of stimulating debate and arriving at a better conclusion.
I am fully aware that this motion involves provincial as well as federal jurisdictions and that in legalistic terms the motion may seem impractical or unenforceable at the federal level. However, I believe that the environmental issue of the day and of years to come which this motion attempts to address, namely, the survival of life on this planet, is of such fundamental importance that Ottawa cannot afford to abdicate any aspect of environmental protection in the name of federal-provincial divisions of power. Pollution problems do not respect political boundaries. The federal government has the advantage of the larger total view of this issue including the long-ranging aspect with will face us at the turn of the century- and perhaps earlier-namely, the disposal of waste.
Furthermore, there are certain questions which all in this country have to address, no matter what implications they might have on such matters as the division of power under the Constitution or the role of the courts. For instance, how much longer can we continue to dump toxic waste into rivers, lakes and oceans before they will be completely unable to regenerate themselves? How much longer will the air be able to cope with pollution from industry, traffic and other sources of pollution? How much longer will the soil be able to absorb increasing amounts of pollution deposited by rain before being irreparably poisoned by man? And who is to blame? We can blame industry for being the villain, we can blame governments for inaction, but in the end it comes back to the inevitable conclusion that the polluter is man. Blame it on the consumer, on western world affluence or on the wasteful society; the fact remains that individually and collectively we are the polluters.
We have conflicting social values here. In each one of us there is the environmentalist who wants to breathe clean air and drink pure water. In each one of us there is also the consumer. Our lifestyles depend on goods and services whose production endangers the very environment we want to protect. These conflicting values find expression in the legislatures and parliaments. Some laws protect the environment, some the consumer and others the capability of industries to make the products we are so eager to buy.
It is for reasons of this kind that I have introduced this motion asking the government to introduce legislation to protect environmental rights. The intent of the motion, in recognizing that as citizens each one of us needs to accept some of the responsibility for the protection of the environment, is to equip the citizen with the tools he or she needs to exercise his or her responsibility, especially when facing big industries, big governments and the consequences of decisions made in faraway places.
The Environment
Barbara Ward summarized this very well when she wrote a few decades ago:
-the warning remains ... if man continues to let his behaviour be dominated by separation, antagonism and greed, he will destroy the delicate balances of his planetary environment. .. once destroyed, there would be no more life for him.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to lend my support and, I think, the support of many of my colleagues for the main thrust of this particular motion, which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing an environmental bill of rights which would, with respect to federal matters-
-accomplish certain ends. I have listened with some real interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) and can agree almost wholeheartedly with the elements which he would like to see in such an environmental bill of rights. They parallel those which have been recommended by various non-government environmental organizations, including the specific recommendations of the Canadian Environmental Law Association in its excellent publication "Environment on Trial". I am referring, in particular, to the chapter on an environmental bill of rights. I take issue with some of the points in the chapter to which I have referred, just as I take issue with a number of those raised by the hon. member for Davenport. But, on the whole, I support the thrust of the suggestions made both by the hon. member and by the Association.
Like the hon. member who has just spoken, I think we do indeed need a bill of environmental rights which, among other things, would state clearly and explicitly that the citizen has the right to a healthy environment, that government has an obligation to protect the environment against individuals or groups who might be predisposed toward violating the environment and that government's first priority in accepting or rejecting any proposal must be the protection of the public interest as far as environmental matters are concerned.
I think such a bill of rights should be backed up with mechanisms and procedures which would make it possible for citizens to participate in all kinds of processes-whether they be tribunals or whatever-established to protect the environment. Just as important as anything else, it is essential that any environmental bill of rights, be it that of the hon. member for Davenport or another, be applicable both federally and provincially.
The fact is that, when the Fathers of Confederation met between 1864 and 1867, they did not see the environment as a matter of great urgency. That was not a failure on their part; it was just a reflection of the reality that environmental issues were not as important then as they are today. The Fathers did not make the relevant provisions; so we have shared jurisdiction over the environment by the federal and provincial governments, with all sorts of attendant problems. For that reason, I think the bill of rights should have application at the two levels.

July 9, 1981
The Environment
Some elements I would like to see in an environmental bill of rights parallel those contemplated by the motion of the hon. member for Davenport. They include the following. First, a clear statement that the public has an inalienable right to a healthy and attractive environment. That fundamental right should be recognized in legislation that would have a degree of paramountcy. At present the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), however well intentioned, has discretion in the application of environmental law. The discretion should be removed or at least severely restricted.
At present, too, the two levels of government may take certain actions to protect the environment, but rarely does legislation state that government must take action. The environmental bill of rights I have in mind would address that problem in such a way that the owner of a particular piece of land or property would be seen to hold it in trust for the public. He or she would handle it knowing that it is not for his or her use only. The individual has an obligation to protect the environment, and failure to respect that public trust would make him or her liable to legal action by the state or by other individuals.
The second element needed is the right of standing. My colleagues in the legal profession could elucidate that concept more eloquently, than I, but let me simply refer to what I envision. It is the right of a citizen to use the law to uphold his common law rights to defend the environment in courts and tribunals. As 1 see it, members of the public should have the right to enforce the law, a right known as standing. Government should not have a monopoly on enforcing environmental protection laws. Certain provisions should be made so that citizens can sue to stop any project, program or policy-or proceeding, for that matter-which is not conducted legally and which harms the environment in some way. Members of the public, individuals or groups, should have the right to appear before government boards, commissions and agencies for this purpose.
A third element is that of environmental impact studies, a requirement that they be done on projects which might endanger the environment before those projects are allowed to proceed. I need not tell the Minister of the Environment how the existing process works; he is across the floor and knows as well as I do. However, for the benefit of other members, there is an initial environmental screening process to determine whether a particular project might have detrimental consequences for the environment. If after that is done there is reason to believe a project would hurt the environment, a more formal review and assessment is done. It is all co-ordinated by the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Office of the Department of the Environment.
The problem is that the process is all discretionary. All of it is done or not done at the whim of the minister or the cabinet, or perhaps on the recommendation of the minister's officials. Even if the minister is well intentioned and has all the goodwill in the world, the fact is that in certain circumstances abuses may happen under the present system. We have already seen how abuses have been allowed to creep in with respect to
the Beaufort Sea. Both the Arctic Waters Advisory Committee, AWAC as it is known, and the Regional Ocean Dumping Advisory Committee, RODAC as it is known, recommended in the strongest terms that certain projects in the Beaufort Sea region not be allowed to proceed until full environmental assessments have been done. I am referring to the circumstances surrounding applications in 1979 for permits for harbour facilities at McKinley Bay and Tuk Harbour.
Well, despite the fact that the government's own advisory committees recommended environmental assessments be conducted, the government proceeded with approval of those permits within only days of the applications being made. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, discretion was exercised without much concern for environmental principles. The inclusion of this particular element in a bill of environmental rights would prevent such an abuse of discretionary power. Governments are always vulnerable to lobbies, special interest groups, and high-powered and well-financed private interests which can manipulate and twist and move the government in one direction or another in their own interest. As a result, the discretionary power of a minister of the environment can sometimes be exercised against the public interest. I think we need public hearings connected with all environmental impact assessments, wherein members of the public who do not have a vested interest in a particular project would have the opportunity to participate fully and without encumbrances. For example, it might be that money will have to be made available for these groups to enable them to take part because it can often be prohibitively expensive to do so otherwise.
There are other provisions, Mr. Speaker, in a bill of environmental rights that I would like to see included. I have already referred to public hearings. In that context, I think freedom of information is vital. The public cannot participate usefully and productively if it is denied information. At present, practically without exception, all information in the possession of government is released to the public at the whim or discretion of a politician or civil servant. No matter how innocuous the information, it requires their approval to be released. Members of this House know from experience that, more often than not, even innocuous pieces of information are marked secret, confidential or restricted.
We need a provision in an environmental bill of rights which opens up the process to the public and allows citizens to have full access to information, with restrictions clearly specified and limited and perhaps with some deterrents to ensure that the system is not abused by the public. Sunshine should be shed on government at a time when all too often darkness prevails.
Public participation should be extended also to the setting of standards. Environmental standards are now largely found in regulations, provided for in some piece of legislation but not detailed there. But practically no one knows what the regulations are because, after the legislation is passed in Parliament, public servants get together, draw up the regulations, and no
July 9, 1981

one ever hears of them. The process needs to be opened up. If there are to be regulations, let them be made public and let them also be devised only after members of the public have been allowed an opportunity to participate in the drafting of them.
My argument is particularly true, for example, in relation to Bill C-48, which is now before committee. Clause 49 will establish an environmental studies revolving fund. Millions of dollars will be disbursed to fund environmental studies to protect the environment against certain resource activities on Crown lands. The regulations which will govern the operation of the fund are not now known to members of Parliament. The specific regulations are not being discussed in the standing committee. They will perhaps never be known to the public. In any event, when they are finally drawn up, they will not reflect any input from the public. An environmental bill of rights needs to take into account that kind of problem.
Also, an environmental bill of rights should make provision for an ombudsman, either an individual or a group. If it is to be a group, it could be an existing environmental body restructured to do a number of things. It would advise the government and the public on environmental matters. It would act as a watchdog on the environment, and it would report periodically on environmental issues.
A further environmental bill of rights provision would give the right to pursue class actions to the public, non-government environmental groups and others. Any citizen or group of citizens would then be able to sue on behalf of similarly aggrieved citizens for any damage resulting from environmental destruction. This might be particularly relevant in connection with hazardous wastes, as the hon. member for Davenport implied.
Another provision in an environmental bill of rights should be the right to defend the environment at reasonable cost. Public participation in tribunals can be prohibitively expensive, as I have already indicated. Individuals and groups will have to be assisted with their participation. We need a mechanism to allocate funds to members of the public who wish to defend the environment through the courts or tribunals.
A further provision should be a restriction on the discretion of environmental agencies. Too often environmental agencies are able to operate unfettered, unbridled and in secret without their decisions being made public or without any provision for public participation in those decisions.
The hon. member for Davenport referred to a judicial review of administrative action. I wholeheartedly concur with his suggestions along those lines. Decisions by government environmental agencies should not be unfettered. These agencies are now allowed to operate almost ex cathedra; they have the last word on the subject and their decisions are usually beyond the reach of courts. I do not think the courts should be allowed to trample upon government agencies or departments. These agencies must be allowed a certain amount of independence. But surely their decisions should not be totally beyond
The Environment
the purview of the courts. The courts should have some role in ensuring that at least due process is followed.
Finally, I think the burden of proof in environmental matters should be on the polluter. I agree with the hon. member for Davenport in that respect. Anyone who wants to introduce a new product, process or substance into the marketplace should be required to demonstrate that it respects the environment. The onus should not be on the public to demonstrate that a certain product or substance will violate the environment. The onus should be on the industry or the company introducing the product into the marketplace to demonstrate clearly beforehand that the environment will be respected.
May I conclude by expressing some regret that the government opposite did not see fit to include environmental rights in its constitutional reform package. It is an irony, with all due respect to the minister, that the Minister of the Environment was asked to assume special responsibilities for piloting the constitutional program through the House and ultimately through Britain, yet the same minister apparently has not had enough clout in cabinet to ensure that the reform package included, if not an environmental bill of rights, then some environmental provisions. Nevertheless, I respect the minister's dedication to the environment and am sure it will be reflected in his remarks this afternoon to which I very much look forward.

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, First I congratulate the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for a passionate and compelling speech. Also I congratulate the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan). I do not agree with all the interpretation which he places upon the present situation, but nevertheless 1 think his speech was constructive and useful and one which I will study with great interest.
I want to particularly congratulate the hon. member for Davenport for bringing this motion before the House. Surely it is an appropriate time, when the country is on the threshold of the establishment of a constitutional entrenchment of the protection of our rights, that our attention should be directed by him to the notion of applying the idea of rights to an environmental bill of rights.
It is a pleasure for me to welcome his motion and to indicate that it has my complete and loyal support, even though in one or two places of detail there may be a certain reservation on my part, at least until we have had a chance to examine further and reflect upon his proposals. Both he in his motion and the hon. member for Hillsborough have stressed the point that we are dealing with an area of responsibility in which there is a shared jurisdiction. I want to touch upon that point for a moment.

July 9, 1981
The Environment
The provinces enact environmental protection laws under the property and civil head of the Constitution, the federal government primarily under its peace, order and good government powers, fisheries, criminal law and the trade and commerce powers. Thus, both levels of government may enact environmental protection laws. In so far as we are able, we would like to act co-operatively with our provincial colleagues in ensuring that in our jurisdiction our actions complement one another and lead to effective action to combat polluting effects.
A few days ago in the House, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), speaking on behalf of the New Democratic Party I think, expressed the concern that there is not a sufficiently clear definition of federal responsibilities in those areas and that there may be some difficulties in leaving such extensive powers in the hands of the provincial governments as there are at the present time. I think that the reference was particularly to the Clean Air Act and the question of transboundary, that is to say, cross-provincial boundary situations of airborne pollution.
I have taken seriously the comments of the hon. member for Brant, and also the kinds of representations which have been made by my colleague, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I would like to say to them and to all hon. members of the House that we have seriously under consideration the question of how the various environmental laws on which federal responsibility is based might be improved, strengthened and clarified, not only in terms of provincial and federal jurisdictions but also in terms of the responsibility for that mandate among the various departments of the federal government. Therefore, it is particularly helpful for me to have the kind of comments which have been expressed today, because within my department, and certainly in my own thoughts, active consideration is being given to exactly how we can strengthen the environmental base for the federal government's action.
The motion that the hon. member for Davenport has brought forward implies that Canadians are denied, or at least may find it difficult to assert, because of the procedural barriers in civil law, the right to seek redress for harm done to them based on environmental wrongs. I can tell your Honour that my departmental officials and I have been examining the difficulties which citizens encounter when they want to make their views known on environmental issues and when they seek redress in the courts. As well, as I have mentioned, examination is being undertaken of the existing federal environmental protection legislation with a view to designing a better, more enforceable and more relevant legislative basis for Environment Canada's environmental protection authorities. Those studies, which are nearing completion, deal directly with many of the issues which the hon. member for Davenport has usefully drawn to the attention of the House today.
First, I should say to the hon. member that Environment Canada expects to implement a department-wide policy which
was first proposed last summer, under which the Department of the Environment will provide for regular and continued consultations between my officials and any and all members of the public. Both of the previous hon. members who have taken part in the debate have stressed the importance of consultation and of widening the basis of consultation. As part of our new proposals, all our important regulations will be reviewed, using clear, equitable and written procedures which will ensure full opportunity for public input at various stages in the regulationmaking process.
There is an important principle which goes far beyond our desire to ensure that the processes of government, such as regulation-making in the environmental protection area, are open and accessible to the public. Let me elaborate on that. When our approach to developing environmental protection regulations was formulated in the early seventies, Environment Canada took great pains to initiate detailed technical discussions with industry in order to identify regulatory requirements which were feasible and which represented the upper limits of good industrial technology and environmental design. The hon. member for Davenport has referred to that process and expressed some skepticism in regard to it, and I think he is right.
In an era when technical requirements established by governments tended to be formed somewhat in a vacuum, there was a risk of legal challenge. I think that in that context, the approach of government-industry task forces was a significant step forward. However, with the benefit of hindsight, I think we can now recognize that that earlier approach, however innovative and progressive it may have seemed in the early seventies, opened the door to the criticism, which was exactly that which the member made, that polluters had a disproportionate influence in the decision-making process, and that the regulations which were issued sometimes may have had the appearance of-and may, indeed, have not only had the appearance but have in substance simply accommodated the needs of industry while providing a kind of symbolic reassurance to a concerned and apprehensive public. I think that the hon. member's criticisms from that point of view are very well taken.
Our new approach to public consultation will welcome and, indeed, will see participation from all concerned public groups. It will provide a much better balance, and, in my view, constitutes a significant feature in Environment Canada's contribution to regulatory reform. I hope that more effective consultation at the rule-making stage will breed better regulations and may reduce the number of occasions on which the enforcement of activity ends up in the courts. I appreciate that public consultation requires calls for innovative approaches. We need to look for and to create new opportunities and discuss policies and programs with those who are either directly or indirectly concerned. We need to have that open dialogue at earlier stages than we have had before in the development of new policies and programs.
I recognize as well that travel costs to effect this consultation can be a burden for some interest groups. I might add that
July 9, 1981

I am pleased to have read that the parliamentary task force on regulatory reform, chaired by my colleague, the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) was encouraged by, and saluted the progressive approach to regulation-making which was being put in place by Environment Canada officials.
My department's new public consultation policy will also include a section on information availability which will be enforced until supplemented by new legislation such as is embodied in the access to information bill which is currently before the committee of the House. I am particularly proud of these initiatives of Environment Canada and feel that they present the vanguard of open and accessible government procedures.
The second point I would like to make is that I am pleased to report that Environment Canada has commissioned a study, which is almost complete, on the general problem of citizen access to the courts in environmental matters. By way of background on this study being done for us, let me remind Your Honour that environmental protection laws have been broadly characterized as common law or statute law. Common law consists of a compilation of reported decisions of judges on disputes resolved earlier, as Your Honour knows. Statute laws are creatures of the legislature and are usually seen as society's legislative statements of a problem. They generally propose a cure for that problem, aimed at controlling and shaping individual behaviour to conform with acceptable societal norms. The controlling devices used are normally regulatory or quasi-criminal in nature. Statute laws are seldom concerned with the rights of a single individual as these have been historically established through the case law associated with civil and property right.
The public should be able to play an important pollution control role at the enforcement level. In Canada, the courts have recognized the right of the individual to enforce the quasi-criminal provisions of regulatory statutes and private prosecution. Your Honour may be aware of the facts associated with a private prosecution concerning pollution problems in the Fraser River in British Columbia. That public action was initiated pursuant to pollution provisions of the Federal Fisheries Act.
I am encouraged that public concern has the outlet, through features of the Federal Fisheries Act, which facilitates the private initiation of legal action. The work on this matter tends to convince me that there should be an increased role for citizen actions on behalf of the Crown to help draw immediate attention and, indeed, to permit the citizen, or any group of citizens, to commence a legal proceeding for the violation of environmental legislation or regulation. I believe that this is a very important principle which the hon. member for Davenport wishes to have us affirm.
One can argue that it should also be possible to use common law causes of action in instances of environmental degradation in order to advance the broader community interest in environmental protection. The prospect of success in privately initiated litigation may be remote due to differing bases of liability, a potpourri of different defences and many proce-
The Environment
dural evidentiary difficulties. For example, in some actions the responsible party's fault is relevant, while in others, liability follows irrespective of whether there is any fault. Often, in order to be successful, a plaintiff must prove that it was the defendant's activity that caused the injury being claimed; or the injuries suffered must be material. In an effort to characterize the injury as material, the plaintiff seeking to advance community interests finds himself on the horns of a dilemma because many of the more pervasive environmental concerns relate to quality of life, to air quality, to quietness, to aesthetics, the lack of which will tend to be characterized by the courts not as material but as little more than personal discomfort. In an attempt to elevate those concerns to the status of material injury, plaintiffs are frequently forced to relate the injuries to their property by showing a general decline in property value.
In spite of some relatively strong judgments from some judges, the trend in Canada seems to be that courts are reluctant to tackle what they regard as the broader social issues. This means that they will tend to favour the economic interests of those who have invested heavily in a project and look to some other agency to strike the appropriate balance of environmental protection and economic development; that is to say, that they will push the determination of that issue outside the context of legal decision. Generally speaking, common law actions are designed to protect property interests, so it follows that one needs some interest in the affected property to maintain the action of a plaintiff under common law.
I would like to abbreviate my remarks on this point, because my simple point is to establish some of the difficulties that we might have if we pursue the objective of relying upon the courts to make some of these decisions concerning the public interest in environmental matters. If we wish to facilitate civil action in the area of environmental protection, we must address those procedural impediments, making it difficult or impossible, and I will quote from the hon. member's resolution, for:
-an individual or group of individuals to initiate court action ... without first having to prove that they have suffered personal or economic damage.
In view of the constitutional considerations, I believe it is the provinces that must take a lead role, since property, civil rights and the administration of justice including civil procedures, are clearly within their domain and constitutional responsibility. I mean that the provinces must take the lead role in relation to the first matter brought to our attention by the hon. member in his resolution.
The second feature of the hon. member's motion proposes as follows:
2. shift the burden of proof to the polluter after the individual or group has established that damage to the environment is likely;

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening following three speakers who have fortunately, or unfortunately covered the waterfront. As is the case when partisanship falls by the wayside and members on all sides of the House deal with an issue in which they have conviction, the first few speakers usually deal with all the vital issues involved.
Let me say that I support this bill. But I want to share a few thoughts and make a few comments on this bill. I have had the privilege of working with some of the members who have spoken who serve on the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services. I recognize the non-partisan kind of work and the sincere attempt which was made by all parties to come up with a solution that is represented in the bill we have before us this evening. The matter has been of concern to us and it has been gnawing away at many members for a considerable period of time. We have already heard about the justice that is represented by this bill.
Not long ago I had the honour to be elected by my peers from my caucus to represent the Ontario members who have a sub-caucus on this side of the House. Sitting as their chairman, I have had the opportunity on many occasions to discuss with members, particularly the younger ones who have come to the House recently, some of the difficulties that we endure together. I might mention some things that have already been
talked about. Collectively we have to come up with second homes. But there are other small and insignificant things which create a need far greater than is apparent to most people from the outside looking in. Any home, no matter where it is located, requires the ordinary upkeep, such as, for example, the cleaning of downspouts, the repairing of sidewalks and painting and fixing of windows from time to time. These may seem insignificant tasks, but when one considers the life of a member of Parliament, if he or she is doing what that member is required to do, which is to be here in Ottawa for the sittings of the House, for committee meetings, for meetings with lobby groups and, when they get home, to attend meetings with their constituents, one realizes that there is very little time to do these extra things. As a consequence, one finds oneself paying someone else to do them.
I have no difficulty in explaining to my constituents as do others, where the tax free allowance goes. When I talk to my constituents who are salesmen, businessmen, junior executives or farmers, and I have a large farming community in my area, people recognize they have certain tax deductible expenses that a member of Parliament does not have available to him. What salesman or trucker does not have some kind of expense allowance while on the road? Does anyone suggest that that person is augmenting his salary or wage by the amount spent while on the job? 1 think not. Therefore, 1 believe that the all-party agreement represents an understanding by this House that there is a definite need and an element of justice that is being responded to. That is represented as well in terms of the agreement on a limited debate. It is probably represented as well by the few exceptions we will hear to the general agreement that we move forward.
I have had the opportunity, as have many members, to examine in depth the Mclsaac-Balcer report. This report set out a middle of the road approach which was neither niggardly nor excessive. Notwithstanding that happy middle ground which the Mclsaac-Balcer report came up with, we in the House, recognizing that there are still examples to be given by the representatives here and willing and prepared to give that kind of example, agreed to accept something considerably less than what Mclsaac-Balcer recommended.
Hon. members will recall the last time we dealt with this issue in 1975. We are now trying to bring at least the base back up to the point where it should have been for the last three or four years. In 1975, salaries were brought to the point where they were at a level where they probably belonged. We then decided that we were going to do without the first increment given to us by reason of the conditions which existed at that time and by reason of the example we were prepared to give.
Few people remember that, except for those who continue to suffer from the fact that we gave that example. It is important that we raise it again. A full year of increment has been missing since 1975 when the legislation was passed. Although we may not suffer in terms of what is in our pockets now, we
July 9, 1981

make those people suffer whom we have either brought with us to Ottawa or who support us in our ridings, be they wives or husbands.
At the time of entering politics, we had a certain standard of living. We had no right to expect our spouses or families to suffer a deteriorating standard of living because of our being here. We did not believe that by coming here we would increase our standard of living. I ask the question rhetorically: would it be fair to expect them to sustain a decrease in that standard of living because of our commitment and their commitment to allow us to come here and offer our services, whatever value they may be, to our country?
My final point by way of delineation is I do not believe that by salary alone we would attract people to devote their time and indeed their lives to the service of their country by serving either this Parliament or another legislative house. I firmly believe it can be a deterrent to persons whom we want to be here making the judgment. As other speakers before me have stated, there should not be a financial impediment to attracting people or at least to making it unattractive for them to present themselves as candidates.
Members on all sides of this House want to do the very best for Canada. We want the best in terms of representatives who will be attracted to this place. The fact that we are dealing with salaries and pensions will help. We do not put at risk to as great an extent, even though there is a sacrifice to be made, the lives of individuals who choose to come here in the future. Without this, those who give it a lot of thought may not come.
I would not want anything I have said to be misinterpreted by my colleagues here or anyone outside this House. I would not want anyone to think I wish I had not done what caused me to come here nor anyone to believe that I am now somehow crying sour grapes. Like every member of this House, I am extremely proud to have been sent here. I came of my own free will after a lot of hard work, not only on my part but on the part of many people in my constituency. I continue to take pride in that and to appreciate it. However, I say at the same time that what we do tonight will permit someone to follow in my footsteps and the footsteps of my colleagues who will be replaced as time goes on by, hopefully, people of even better calibre and quality. They will not be, among other things, jeopardizing the standard of living which they and their families will have.
I will be supporting this bill. I compliment the House leader for having brought it forward and I compliment my colleagues on both sides of the House who worked so hard to draft what has ultimately come before us this evening.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will speak briefly on this bill because many of the points I wish to enunciate have already been covered. At the outset I will state my position because I think it is important. I feel very strongly that this bill is long overdue. I am going to support the bill. 1 am going to vote for the bill.
I want to say publicly what I have said privately in the corridors and outside this House. I do not believe that mem-
Senate and House of Commons Act bers of Parliament are adequately paid. At the same time I am in a distasteful position. I find it distasteful to speak to a matter where I am the arbiter in which I have a personal interest. There is a certain sense of unfairness. As members of Parliament, we must do something to ensure that this does not occur time and time again.
This problem has been before us on numerous occasions. Many members of Parliament thought there was some type of panacea or solution in having a report prepared whereby independent people would provide us with suggestions as to amounts for our salaries, pensions and other matters. Unfortunately what happens with respect to these matters is it is always a source of political embarrassment.
Every political party in this House has a certain concern about what the political fallout will be when we begin talking about matters in which we have a direct personal interest. If we learn anything as a result of this bill and what has preceded it, it is that the type of reform we need, not only for members of Parliament but judges and deputy ministers, is a different process for determining the proper amount of salaries and benefits to be afforded senior officials of government.
This problem is not new in the world. The Australians have a far more preferable system than the one we have to endure tonight and throughout the ages of Parliament when it comes to this issue. The Australians appoint a tribunal. It is not made up of civil servants but of people who have been out of politics in an elected way for more than seven years. They meet every year and advertise their hearings. The government actually makes representations as to what the proper amount of salary and additional benefits ought to be. Then within 15 days of a decision being made, unless 50 per cent of the house signs a petition and puts it before the house in Australia, that is what the salaries are.
It is high time this Parliament stopped spending its time dealing with matters which involve not only our own salaries but also the salaries of judges. I think that is not the proper course Parliament should adopt, and we ought to do something constructive about it. I think the Australians are on the right track. The people of New Zealand have adopted the Australian course of action. We should seriously look at that as a pattern, not only for establishing our own salaries but also the salaries of judges and the salaries of senior civil servants.
With respect to the amounts we are talking about, may I say that the government has not arbitrarily set our salaries. Salaries were suggested by a commission established for that purpose. The amount we are about to receive, as the last speaker so accurately pointed out, is two-thirds of what this independent tribunal assessed, and still within this House there is a sense of embarrassment because we have to speak about it in terms of our own personal interests. That is just not right.
I was very much impressed when we were discussing the Judges Act. Representations were made to all of us with respect to what the proper salaries of judges ought to be. I was one of the members of Parliament who spoke to judges. They

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act
pointed out the hardship they were personally enduring as a result of making $60,000 a year. We know what judges make now, close to $80,000 for judges at the superior court level and $70,000 at the county court level. Yet complaints were made to me in good faith that they could not send their kids to college and that they were finding it financially embarrassing. In addition to that-and every member of this House is aware of it-they wanted a pension to which they would not have to contribute. That matter was a source of deep contention in this House. We hived off that bill, and that matter will now be decided within committee. I put it to the House that if judges found it hard to support their families at $60,000, how is a member of Parliament to carry out the responsibilities of supporting his family at $32,000?
There are certain members of this House who are independently wealthy and do not worry about salary. There is a good number of us who have to worry because it is now our only source of income. I am a lawyer by profession, but I do not practise law any more because the responsibilities of a member of Parliament are such that I do not have the time. It used to be different but it is not that way now, and I think our constituents demand that we spend full time in this House. I do not want to be handsomely paid; I want to be adequately compensated.
As I see the suggestion in the bill before us, which is two-thirds of what an independent tribunal assessed, I think there can be no argument in this House that we are being overpaid that meets the test of reason. There is no just way we are. With respect to the matter of salary I wholeheartedly endorse this bill.
Let me speak about a matter which I find in the newspapers constantly, the fact that in addition to the $32,000 we receive as salary we also receive a tax-free allowance. People say that is part of our salary. I for one want to tell those people who think that is the case that it is just utter nonsense. I believe there are members in this House who will agree with me when I say that we spend every cent of our tax-free allowances and more. I do not consider that to be salary at all. I hope the public understands that members of Parliament actually do use that for maintaining homes and for the expenditures pointed out by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) which are incidental to our being members of Parliament. I think everyone in this House is proud of the privilege of representing his own constituency. It is a good feeling to wake up in the morning and to like going to work, in spite of the frustrations.
Nobody here is a member of the House of Commons for the money. That is clear, but what is not clear to many people is that members of Parliament in many cases are hurting a great deal, and they ought to be adequately compensated.
The final point I wish to make is in relation to the very interesting and useful part of this bill respecting severance. To me a 50 per cent severance allowance is a welcome addition. I had a pretty good law practice when I was practising in Cambridge in southwestern Ontario, but if I were to go back to the practice of law and take up where I left off, it would
take me at least a year to establish my clientele again. No matter how prominent a member is, when he goes back into business, law, medicine or dentistry, it takes time. To my way of thinking, one-half of the salary is certainly a welcome addition.
The last matter I would like to address is the question of the pension. I re-emphasize what the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton stated. I make a certain assumption, and that assumption is that the pension is responsibly funded. We have the assurance of the government on this matter and, that being the case, I lend my wholehearted support to this bill, which I think is long overdue.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks by expressing my thanks to my colleagues for agreeing that I might be the second speaker of this party for, as will be expected by almost everyone, it is my intention to speak against this bill and to vote against it when the debate ends.
I want also to thank the government House leader for suggesting this afternoon that both the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and I have been co-operative in arranging for this debate to take place. That is true for both of us, but I would like it to be clear that my co-operation was because I believe in the right of the members of this House to discuss the matter if they wish to do so, and I was happy to lend my co-operation to make that possible. That does not mean I am co-operating for the purpose of getting the bill passed. It was understood-and I am grateful for this-that even if only one member were to stand at the end of the debate to request a recorded vote, there would be such a recorded vote.
Another complimentary word I should like to offer is to my friend, the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), for the speech he made this afternoon. He knows I do not agree with him, but I thought he made a well stated and excellent case for the bill and for the position of members of Parliament. I thought he did it-and I say this very deeply and sincerely-without giving any offence to those of us who might take the other side of this issue.
Nevertheless, having said that, I disagree with most of the arguments which have been put forward and, in my view, Parliament ought not to be passing this bill at this time.
I suppose I am a different breed. A couple of years ago the Prime Minister referred to Tommy Douglas and me as leftovers from the depression. Tommy Douglas had an appropriate retort. I made none. I did not mind the suggestion the Prime Minister had made, namely, that some of us have not forgotten the experience people went through in that decade. I suppose if I tell you that I also was born into depression in 1908 and that I graduated from university in 1930 into another depression, members will say: Oh, that explains Stanley. He has had too much of that kind of background.
July 9, 1981

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext: That is not true. We all went through it.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that, and I am glad 1 have not forgotten those experiences. However, I also feel that I must never forget why I came to this institution. I must never forget the conditions under which so many of my constituents still live. I like to think my constituents are not just those who live within the boundaries of Winnipeg North Centre, but they are pensioners, veterans and people in need right across Canada. I feel I must not forget them.
As I say, it was because of what I went through, what I saw people going through in the 1930s, that I decided I had to move from the pulpit into politics, and eventually found my way here in 1942 for the purpose of achieving greater equality amongst the people of Canada, and to solve some of the economic problems our people face. In my view, Mr. Speaker, and I hold this very deeply, if I am going to remember the people out there, there must not develop too wide a gulf between my standard of living and theirs. I speak only for myself, I do not ask anyone else to agree, but I feel if I am going to represent the people in need, the pensioners, the veterans and all the rest, they must not feel there is such a gulf between us that I cannot really mean it. I am not suggesting members of Parliament have to be poor or go into debt and all that sort of thing. But I am suggesting it does not hurt one whit for us to experience a few difficulties and know what life is like in economic terms if we are to represent faithfully the people out there who are suffering economic difficulties.
I recognize the case that has been made, particularly by my friend, the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody whom I have already complimented, for the needs of many of our members, especially the younger ones with families. However, the Prime Minister has already said that older people should rearrange their priorities and somehow get along. If we want to maintain contact and credibility with our people, we should rearrange our priorities, even on our $47,100 combined salary and expenses allowance we now receive and try to make it. I do not equivocate about the matter at all. I think the pay and allowances we are now receiving should stay at that level and we should not at this point be seeking an increase. I say that at this time in particular because of the difficult circumstances facing Canadians in recent months. The tremendous increases in the cost of living and interest rates have put our people in a difficult position, and we in this place have done very little to ameliorate their situation. I do not think it brings us closer to them to ameliorate our situation when we have done nothing for them.
I want to be fair about this session. I do not see very much that we have done at all. There was that $35 increase in the guaranteed income supplement last summer which has been eaten up time and again so far as our older people are concerned. Tomorrow we will pass a bill that I have been pleading for every week this year to cut out the delay in benefits sour 20,000 widows of veterans were subjected to in the bill we passed last summer. Now, if other members can add to that list the things we have done to meet the needs of the people we represent, I would be glad to hear them.
Senate and House of Commons Act

speechtext: Silence.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT

speechtext:
I hear silence, just as if I were performing a wedding and had asked if anyone had anything to say, let him say it now or forever hold his peace. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we say that we, too, have troubles: the high cost of mortgages, interest rates, the cost of living, cost of travel. However, we are in a position to do something about it. It can be justified; everyone who has spoken in this debate thus far has justified it. I say, and I speak only for myself, that I do not want to be in the position of improving my situation when we have done so little for those out there.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I cannot vote for this bill. As I say, quite frankly-and I do not apply this test to anyone else-I cannot retain for myself the extra dollars that would come to me if this bill were passed. I feel it all very deeply. I have already made reference to what my experience has been. My friend, the hon. member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) says we have all had those experiences. That is true. I am not the only person in this place who came from humble beginnings and who know the experience of a shop worker father who was laid off from time to time. I am not the only one; this place has many persons like that. I just do not want to forget it. I think this Parliament should not forget it, and I think we would better represent the people of Canada if we ourselves deliberately suffered a bit, if we deliberately delayed doing things for ourselves until more has been done for the people we represent. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I feel this bill should not be passed.
I am not trying to answer the arguments that have been made. They are all valid. It depends on the point of view from which you start. I think someone said today, what is the job worth? What are the people prepared to pay? My question is: What am I prepared to pay to maintain the confidence of the people for whom I am working here and not just to get something better for myself? I am prepared to pay the price I have implied in what I have already said.
It is sometimes argued that a better rate of pay is necessary in order to attract good people to the House of Commons. I think that is nonsense. I was going to use another word but the Prime Minister did not like it when my leader used it earlier today.

speechtext: No, no. In my view, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, and it has been quoted, I have never seen any lack of candidates at election time, and everyone knows then what the pay is going to be. I can remember some awfully good men in Parliament when the pay was $4,000 a year and no extras.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
