speechtext:
Yes, $1 men also. I know times have changed, but my fear is that getting the salaries up where they are and where they are going-and these figures are getting pretty high by the time you add in the new salary level, the tax free expense allowance, and the higher indexing, within a few years

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act
we will be up there in the stratosphere-all it really does is attract people looking for a good paying job. I think for the good of the country we should avoid that. Maybe others will say: Well, I am just like the rest; I do not want it to be too high or too low. However, I think the emphasis, the main reason for coming here, should be one of dedication to the good of the country and of the people we represent. We may not forget them with more money in our pockets, but they think we will. They think we are in the position of the elite and that we have ail kinds of things that we do not even have. It seems to me that we should be prepared to pay a price to have the confidence of the people we represent. That, to me, is something which is very important about Parliament these days. People are wondering whether we really represent them, whether we are really addressing ourselves to their problems. They are coping with 20 per cent interest rates, they are coping with food costs which have gone sky high, they are coping with housing problems that they cannot meet, and all the rest of it. I just have the fear that in the next day or two, as people read about what we have done today, they will feel, "Well, those men and women have taken care of themselves. Can we count on them addressing themselves to our needs?"
I am speaking only for myself. I say again that 1 am grateful to my colleagues, the majority of whom are on the other side of the issue, for letting me speak at this time. If we cannot make my way prevail, if we cannot get the bill defeated, I hope that at least I will inspire people to the proposition that we must think a lot more about what we are doing for the people we represent.
I know one could say, "We will do this first and then we will do it for the others". It does not normally work that way, but I want some sense of conscience to be felt in the House about what we are doing. I know all the arguments, that the $4,000 which I talked about when I was first here is irrelevant. I may say to the younger ones who are having difficulty that I understand it. I knew what it was to try to get by on a $4,000 indemnity with Mr. Ilsley taking $1,200 of it away in income tax during the war, with no air flights to get home, only railway passes, with out-of-pocket expenses which paid for two trips a year. Boy, look at the distance we have come. Look at the things we have now as part of our jobs. They also add to our standard of living, to the joy of being here, to the thrill of being members of Parliament. 1 suppose it has been decided in each caucus how the vote will go tonight, that the bill will pass, but I want to express my objection to it.
One of the other arguments used of course is that in terms of percentages the increases that we have had in the last few years add up to something like 4.5 per cent per year and that the people out there have been receiving higher average increases than those. Let us remind ourselves that it depends upon the base, it depends upon where it is starting. I have this argument with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) about old age security. She and the rest of the government are proud that the pensions are indexed according to the rise in the consumer price index. The base to begin with
was too low. With us the base to begin with back in 1974-75 was way ahead of the average, and we received increases. The thing to look at is not a comparison of the rate of increase but the absolute dollars and the absolute relationship between us and the people we represent. If we do that, I hope we will think more about the whole situation.
As I say, I do not expect to change the vote. I am glad the government House leader and the opposition House leader agreed with me yesterday that we would have a vote so that those of us who feel as I do could have our votes recorded against this bill. At least I hope the thoughts I am uttering will have some effect on the thinking of members and that, starting tomorrow, starting next week, or starting on October 14 when we come back, we will try to be better representatives of the people, with members more attentive to their needs if for no other reason than for conscience sake because of what we have done for ourselves.
While I am on my feet may I say that there are one or two things I would have liked to raise in committee on the bill. I realize by the time 9.45 p.m. comes, there will still be members wanting to speak on second reading and the committee stage will be quite pro forma. If I have anything I want to say in terms of the things that are in the bill, I will have to say them now.
The first is that I am very sorry that with this bill being brought in, opportunity was not taken to correct something for former members of Parliament who retired a number of years ago for whose wives there is no protection if the member died first. There are only about 20 or 25 such former members, all of whom I knew; they were here in my time. They retired and went on the small pension that it was then, $3,000 per year being the maximum, but it was before there was a provision for survivors. There are these 20 or 25 former members out there who are prepared to make payment to cover actuarially the cost of a pension for their widows. They have been in correspondence with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and with the government House leader. It has been kicked around. I have had copies of most of the letters. I had thought when the time came to amend the Members of Parliament Retirement Allowances Act that something would be done. We are doing things in this bill, especially in the pensions part, for members who are now here. We are permitting them to go back and make extra payments for years gone by so as to get the full advantage of this bill, but why is it that we are never prepared to do something for those who have left the place? As I said, the 22 or 23 former members about whom I am talking are quite prepared to pay the actuarial amounts to cover their widows. I wish something had been done for them.
Speaking of the pension arrangements, I have to say that through all the fine arguments I have heard defending the new pension arrangements I found it pretty hard to accept as justifiable a scheme under which in 15 years one can become qualified for what is known as a full pension. The argument is that members pay for it. They pay for it out of the increased indemnity. Actually we pay for half of it; the government puts up the other half. Any steel worker or any elementary school
July 9, 1981

principal in the country would be happy to pay for a pension that good-fully matured at the top level in 15 years. It has been agreed to. If it goes through now I think it is a little too much. If I may return to my theme, I hope after it is done that we will have a little conscience and realize that having done what we have for ourselves, we ought to be doing a lot more for the people we represent.
By the same token-and I would have raised this in Committee of the Whole had there been time to do so-I still think that it does not make sense and it is not fair that a pension for life is available regardless of one's age. I know it is hypothetical and theoretical, but it is possible for a person to be elected here at the age of 18, spend six years as a member and receive a pension for life, level up to age 60 and indexed thereafter. No one has done that, but there are members who have gone out in their thirties and forties, and there will probably be more. This does not happen in ordinary society. People say, "Why do you do those things for yourselves when you will not do them for us?" It has been my experience that after almost every time we have done something to the pension plan, some Liberal has come to me and said that we should not have done that. I remember particularly when we had the Curtis report a number of years ago. Professor Curtis of Queen's did one of the studies, and one of the things he recommended, I think, was that members' pensions be deferred to age 55. Some have suggested age 50, but certainly it should be age 55 or 60. While it was before us we got nowhere. I suspect within a few days from now there will be some members saying that that is what we should have done, and so we should have. These are things I would have raised had we got into committee of the whole. That will be a pro forma experience, so I mention them now.
I will be a bit more personal. I have heard two or three hon. members say today that it is an honour to be here but that families cannot live on honour. I know that is true. It is not my suggestion that we should ask them to do that. It is not my suggestion that we reduce the indemnity. I would take it if there were a reduction, but I guess I am that strange breed. But I want to say that you could not pay me with millions of dollars to match the satisfaction I have had in being a member of Parliament. I was here for 16 years, from 1942 until 1958. I had a four-year break, and I have been here 19 years since then. So I have been in this House for 35 years. In the first session that I was here, I think the first accomplishment that I won-and hon. members will smile about this in view of what will happen tomorrow-was a concession from the Hon. Ian MacKenzie. He was then minister of pensions and national health, and he had charge of veterans affairs. The department had not yet been created. I pleaded from my seat in the back row, for widows of World War I non-pensioned veterans, for whom there was nothing. They are now covered in the War Veterans Allowance Act. They were not, in those days, even though the act had been around for a number of years.
1 remember the day when Ian MacKenzie got up in this House and tabled an order-in-council which would provide ad
Senate and House of Commons Act
hoc allowance for that year to those widows of World War I veterans. Someone said that it was reported in the paper that I was jumping for joy yesterday. I almost jumped for joy then over the satisfaction of that kind of an experience within a year or two after I came here, in that same first session which ended in 1945. I was not alone then, but I had a good deal to do, by way of participating in it-we got the first increase in the old age pension, which had been $20 a month from 1927 until 1945. Just before the election in 1945, we got that pension increased to $25 a month. There was still a means test. The pension was still paid 75 per cent from Ottawa and 25 per cent from the provinces. Then Manitoba had to be persuaded to pay its $1.25. These amounts sound infinitesimal now, but the thrill of that sort of thing makes the experience of being here, through all of its frustrations and through all of the disappointments, one which one could not match with millions of dollars.
Across the years I have been involved in the same things, such as old age pensions raising them up from that $25 up to where they are now, over $200 on a universal basis at age 65; getting family allowances started and keeping them on a universal basis at a time when the government wanted to put them on a means test. We now have unemployment insurance, hospitalization, medicare, the Canada Pension Plan and greatly improved veterans benefits. I could make a longer list of the things which 1 have not seen succeed; but I say to hon. members; do not think of this place as one where one has to work hard and does not get much pay. Think of it as a place where if one stays with it and has some sense of dedication one can win.
This morning while I was in my office there was hardly half a minute between each of the phone calls which came. Some of them were about today's business and matters like that, but most of them were from people who had seen the item in the news this morning about the bill which was introduced yesterday to end that waiting period for 15,000 or 20,000 veterans' widows. As a matter of fact, I do not think one of the calls was from a widow herself. The calls were from other people, such as veterans and citizens generally who were just pleased that this step had been taken. No sum of money can match that satisfaction.
I do not need a pay increase. I do not need tributes or that sort of thing. The thrill of being here and winning some of these accomplishments, the feeling that people out there are perhaps a little better off in some respects, or that they are glad they have someone who is a friend in court for them, makes this experience, the 35 years that I have had here, such a delight that I hope I can do it again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this intervention will be a short one. It will be one which I do not relish making. First of all, I would like to give thanks for the opportunity of participating in this debate and to explain why, by virtue of perhaps being old-fashioned or by virtue of having a mental block or other reasons which I cannot briefly describe, my reasoning leads me to the conclusion that, regretfully, I cannot support this bill.
This is the way I see the issue. To me it is a question of going back a year ago when I was elected for the life of this Parliament. In a way I felt that I was hired under the terms and the conditions of the duration of this Parliament. I therefore feel that I entered into this role of a member of this House with the clear understanding as to what was ahead of me, both the good and the bad. Having reached this point in my thinking, my next step, therefore, is to comment on the approach which I would support and I would urge the government to consider, because this is not the first time and there will be other times, years from now when this matter will be before this House.
I think we should arrange things in a way whereby one Parliament decides for the next. In our specific case, 1 would be glad to support the measure whereby we would determine the salaries and other conditions for the members of Parliament to be elected in the next Parliament, namely, the thirty-third Parliament. In doing so, I think we would, first, increase the quality of accountability in such a way that it would not harm the texture of democracy, and maybe it would strengthen it. Second, we would be making a decision for a group of parliamentarians whom we really do not know yet, for another group separated from us; some of us may be in that group and some of us may not. In other words, we would not be making a decision for ourselves; we would be making a decision for the next group, whatever the composition of that group may be. Third, the public would know in advance. It might want to make it an issue, but I doubt it very much. However, it would not be an issue which will be raised during the life of a Parliament for that specific Parliament but it would be an issue in relation to the following one. The public would know, the candidates would know, and there would be no element of surprise. I had hopes that this bill would contain a clause which would permit those who wish to do so to continue under
the present regime until the end of the life of this Parliament. In other words, in doing so there would have been an element of choice and a possibility of option. Those who want to continue this regime would be able to do so, and would therefore have a choice. Those who want to have a change, would have the alternative. I regret that this clause has not been included. I would not say that this is the entire picture that I would like to give in my reasoning. There is also one element that has to do with timing. It seems to me that this is not exactly the most appropriate time in relation to what is going on in our economy.
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, my position is that I cannot support this bill. I do support the concept, the principle of one Parliament deciding the income of the next Parliament. As I mentioned before, this is not the first and it may not be the last time when MPs debate their own salaries. Each time it is no fun to see this issue come along this way, no matter on which side of the issue one stands. The concept of accountability, the concept of timing and of the option, are all related to this basic principle of one legislature deciding for the following.
I should like to conclude by saying that like all my, colleagues in this House, I enjoy the parliamentary work. I enjoy the conditions under which I am allowed to work and I regret very much not being able to support the majority of my colleagues in this project.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this pay and pension bill which has seen the light of day in this House this afternoon, hence my handwritten notes, rather hastily put together.
Neither I, nor anyone in this House, has had a chance to inspect and calculate the cost of this pay and pension bill. I find that a very uncomfortable position from which to debate any legislation in the House.
I am certain that the pensioners who are waiting for their cheques and the small business owners who are watching their businesses atrophy, will not be impressed at the way we suddenly sneaked this bill in and will pass it in the course of six hours over other much more important legislation. I am particularly appalled by the callous disregard of cost associated with the bill, especially in the pension provision. It would have been far better to split pay from pension so that we could have responsibly investigated and debated them individually. Although they are linked, I intend to deal with them separately.
Let me begin with the pay portion and the increases for members. I will say at the outset, that while many of my colleagues have made eloquent speeches in defence of a pay increase and I agree with many of the points, this is a debatable bill and many of those points are debatable.
I regret very much having to speak against the personal and family interest of many members, as they are perceived by them. Perhaps I should say that it is my former colleagues I will be speaking against when tomorrow morning comes
July 9, 1981

around. Indeed, I could have restrained myself from speaking against the bill at all had we simply been debating a pension bill. Let me dispassionately attempt to offer the counter view on some of the reasons advanced by my colleagues for the pay increase. I had intended to discuss the arguments of hard work, long hours, exposure to public ridicule, maintaining two homes, the fact that higher pay would provide better members of Parliament and all that sort of thing, but some of my recent colleagues and speakers here tonight have made the case for me, so I will not waste the time of the House on that.
Let me deal with a couple of arguments to the effect that this pay increase is needed in order to compensate MPs in a manner commensurate with private sector professionals, and that MPs provide a valuable service and do a most important job of running the country. At the risk of seeming to be facetious and cynical, let me examine some of these points.
The comparison with the private sector income and the quality of service in running the country can, I think, be dealt with together. It is true that executive pay is generally greater than that of an MP but, private sector salaries and pay scales are based on the achievement of results. Much has been made today about the activity of members of Parliament. If we are being paid for being busy, or being inconvenienced, or being bothered by the public at any time of the day or night, or for the discomfort in travelling, or all the other arguments, then the public is certainly getting a bargain if we are paid by the hour. But if we are being paid for results, as in the private sector, then I submit there is little justification for a pay increase based on this Parliament's results.
One of my colleagues has argued that individual members have not made claims to control inflation or hold down interest rates or support the value of the Canadian dollar or hold down the price of gasoline, and therefore they cannot be held responsible for failure in these areas. This, I submit, is a specious argument at best. The government certainly did claim it would do these things and every member was a spokesman and a mouthpiece for those claims with his constituents; ipso facto, every member here, whether elected to the government side or not, made or implied such a claim by virtue of running for Parliament at a fee which was known in advance.
Let us look at the one and one third year record of the government, its members and all of us, to see whether we justify and deserve the $9,000 per year pay increase reward for performance for meeting the obligations and promises in the contractual arrangement we made with the public of Canada.
The price of gasoline which was $1.07 per gallon when we were elected, is now $1.60, which is way over the guaranteed maximum. Interest rates on election day were running at 14 per cent but today they are 5 per cent higher, at over 19 per cent. The value of the Canadian dollar was 86 cents on the U.S. dollar on February 18, 1980 but today it is down to below 83 cents on the U.S. dollar. Inflation was running at 9.5 per cent then, is today running at 12.3 per cent and tomorrow we will hear the latest news on that. I submit that does not justify a pay increase at all.
Senate and House of Commons Act
We could look at other economic indicators or yardsticks but I think these are as important as any and will serve. You will agree, Mr. Speaker, that they represent the total failure of this Parliament to achieve the objectives claimed. This does not warrant the reward of a huge pay increase. I suggest that the government side should be penalized by the amount of inflation, not rewarded by its failure to deal with it.
What other Canadians have the opportunity to redress their absolute job failure or to relieve themselves of the burden of high prices by giving themselves an offsetting pay increase? I have heard the argument that inflation cannot be controlled, that it is imported, that it is inevitable, etc. ad nauseam. I suggest that a government which has paid attention to the development of Canadian industry and Canadian production and Canadian jobs over the years would now be seeing the results of sound industrial strategy. These results would have had Canada importing less foreign goods and, therefore, less foreign inflation. We would be producing more domestic goods made from Canadian natural resources and therefore eliminating, to a large degree, the cost of imported inflation. Even if we were importing inflation from our principal trading partner, the United States, that might be a benefit. Their inflation is only two thirds as high as ours.
Even if we do not accept the argument that inflation can be controlled, let me ask; if members of Parliament with the federal government cannot control inflation, who can? This large increase and this increased indexing of both pay and expense allowance will give government members no incentive at all to fight vigorously on behalf of senior citizens, mortgaged home owners, small business people and the people who drive cars and heat homes.
I can just imagine myself going back to my constituents explaining to them how I am down here battling inflation, battling high interest rates on their behalf, while I vote myself an unwarranted-and that is unwarranted by results-pay increase.
Let me now deal with the real issue as I see it, namely pensions. The pension program is a very costly item. This proposal is the most unparliamentary and irresponsible action by a spendthrift government. The government House leader (Mr. Pinard) said earlier that consultation among the parties had preceded the introduction of this bill. That is true. But he neglected to mention that no details had ever been given, certainly not to this party. Indeed, I have never seen any. No discussion with members with regard to detail or cost preceded this debate. We are seeing the bill for the first time today and I consider that irresponsible. No expenditure measure should ever be debated and passed without a detailed examination, in this case a detailed study of the actuarial soundness.
A government which has brought us a $15 billion annual deficit is certainly not one to be looked to for calculating in advance the cost of such an expensive program at the expense of the taxpayer. Surely it would not have been too much to have asked the government chief actuary to inspect. He was

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act not consulted, nor was the superintendent of insurance for Canada.
Actuarial figures, such as the return on investment calculation on the funds invested to see how much there will be when payout takes place, have not been studied. If you look at some of the cost comparisons with the private sector, you will see how bad this is. The average cost of a pension plan in the private sector is about 9 per cent of the total lifetime income of the recipient. Even in the best of private sector plans, the cost is about 12 per cent to 15 per cent of the total lifetime earnings of the pension recipient.
If the salary increases with indexing, and the cost of pensions as shown in the Mclsaac-Balcer report are carried out, the cost down the road to the government, that is the taxpayer, will be something in the order of 75 per cent of the lifetime earnings of a member of Parliament. That is irresponsible. Even if a member pays 10 per cent out of his own pocket, the government will be picking up something over 70 per cent, with the rest coming from investment. The government forbids anyone else in the country, parliamentarians excluded, from earning more than 2 per cent of their lifetime earnings as a pension. That is the law. This plan allows members of Parliament to have pensions as great as 5 per cent of their lifetime earnings, or 2.5 times the amount allowed to a regular Canadian citizen by law. That pension allowance applies from the day a parliamentarian leaves this place and it carries on until a member reaches the age of 60 at which time the pension becomes indexed. It goes upwards from there.
There has never been an evaluation of the members' pension plan. Even the present plan has never been actuarially studied. How could any responsible or informed member support such extravagance? Any 15-year member of Parliament who votes today on this pension plan provision will be voting himself or herself a $250,000 or more increase of lifetime earnings. That is over and above the $700,000 or so that are put away for him already in the present pension plan. Therefore, a member who has been elected for 15 years will have the value of about $1 million set aside in his or her name as pension funds. That is for regular members. Cabinet members will get much more. Even parliamentary secretaries significantly get more, probably $500,000 more than regular members.
In six hours we are sneaking through a $9,000 pay increase as provided for by the Mclsaac-Balcer report which has been cut by one third, which is supposedly a real cutback. The argument was made earlier that what other union or group of Canadian citizens would take less than an arbitrator's recommendation, but I submit that two thirds paid out in full today is better than 100 per cent paid out over four years, if you know anything about 20 per cent money today.
The least we could have done as a government was to consult our two distinguished actuarial former members, one in the Quebec Legislative Assembly and one a former member of this Parliament. They could have looked at this plan on our behalf. Mr. McCrossan was the former member of Parliament for York-Scarborough. Mr. Claude Castonguay is the former minister of health for Quebec and lately is a special adviser to
the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). As adviser to the minister, Mr. Castonguay helped in an intensive investigation into private sector pensions. If it were so important to have looked into private sector plans, would it not have been useful to have consulted Mr. Castonguay on the massive outlay contemplated here today? If the government had not wanted to consult the private sector people, it could have consulted Mr. Walter Reise, chief actuary. He is knowledgeable about RCMP pensions and other public service pensions. He has the computer and the program ready to go, yet he has not been consulted.
How can we study the private sector to death and yet not look even casually into this mammoth expenditure? There is even a federal-provincial conference set up for September to look into the private sector. We are not rushing into that in any six hours.
I implore the government to separate these two items of pay and pensions so that Parliament can inspect the costs and the ramifications of this actuarially unsound and unethically large pension which cannot even be provided under the law to the ordinary citizens.
Finally, let us recognize that by providing such an inordinately large pension after 15 years, an MP will be better off if he or she retires from Parliament, then collects a pension of 75 per cent of the best six years and takes another job. So much for keeping skilled parliamentarians working and getting better members of Parliament.
The government of today does not know and cannot know how many members will retire, will be defeated, how long they will serve or how long they will live an draw pensions, in some cases along with their spouse. So the costs of output cannot be controlled and have not been actuarially studied. Only the input amounts are known.
I intend to vote against this vast and irresponsible disregard of public funds, this unwarranted squandering of the dollars of the citizens of Canada for the benefit of government members of Parliament who are not carrying out their jobs successfully on behalf of the citizens they are sworn to serve. I hope other members will have both the conscience and the good business sense to vote against it as well.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF SENATORS AND MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to break down to some of the arguments just made by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist). I do not know how much schooling he had, but when he states that two thirds now are better than 100 per cent in three years, I think that he should figure it out for himself, and he would then see that, in view of the indexation, this amounts instead to 26 per cent less than what is recommended by the report of the Mclsaac-Balcer Committee. He should learn some arithmetic.
Second, I would like him to note, with regard to his arguments against the pension fund, that the average term of office of a member of Parliament is four and a half years, and that to be eligible for pension, a member of Parliament has to remain
July 9, 1981

in office for six years. When the average term of office is between four and a half and five and a half years and when the first condition to receive a pension is to have remained in office for six years, he can certainly not maintain that this system will favour a certain elite. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if we consider the problem objectively, we can see that a real problem exists because we are all human and no union in Canada would have agreed to settle for an increase of 4.4 per cent in seven years.
One of my colleagues on this side of the House argued that he knew what his salary would be when he agreed to be a candidate. I remember what went on when I was with labour negotiating collective agreements. When I first got a job, I accepted the first offer that the employer made to me. A year later, I was president of the union and I wanted a higher salary for myself and for the others. I therefore think that it is unrealistic to maintain that we entered politics with full knowledge of the conditions and that we must now live with them.
I would like to give a few examples for the benefit of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He quoted the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the beginning of his comments. For my part, I would like to quote Plato, who was a great philosopher and a great politician. Plato said that politics must live with honour. Those who know me will say that it is unusual for me to quote Plato. I especially want to remind the hon. member that Plato was somewhat older than he is and that values have changed as well as practical realities.
When my hon. colleague first came to Parliament I had not even been born. I am sure things have changed since then. I am sure as well that things have been happening outside this House and there are times when I would urge him to go outside a little more often. As to those whose conscience prompts them to speak sincerely against the increase as proposed, I do invite them to get in touch with my office, for I am quite sure that they will find poor people in my riding who will be willing to accept the salary increases which those members find indecent today. I will be pleased to spread it among my electors. In that sense, one must be honest with everybody here. The salary increase we are about to vote for ourselves a little later is quite realistic. We simply have to look at Quebec right now where welders earn $1,300 a week-and they are on strike. They want $2,000 a week. Multiply that by 52 and you get $ 104,000. Those are today's facts of life.
When we came into politics, we wanted to serve the public. We also liked it and were willing to do it. But that does not mean that today we should try to belittle the role of member of Parliament because I for one believe that refusing to give a member of Parliament a decent salary is tantamount to belittling his role. That is quite all right for those who can manage to survive on $4,000 a year or who are so well off that they do not know what it is to be broke. We would then find ourselves
Senate and House of Commons Act within a group of wealthy people and a closed circle of millionaires who will be able to pay their own way, sit here and say: "Yes, we are working because it is an honour".
Mr. Speaker, I see nothing wrong in the fact that men and women in this House decide to accept a proposal which is less generous than the one recommended by an independent committee. I am saying this to you and 1 say it in front of all my colleagues here: I would have liked to get much more. I would have liked us to accept the Balcer report recommendations because he himself said in his report that those were minimum levels; and yet, keeping in mind the economic rather than the political situation, we have already agreed that perhaps it might be more normal to cut that increase by one third. I do not know many people who have offices and who work outside the House, who would go along with a cut of perhaps one third in their income.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I do not feel ashamed to take part in the vote tonight, because I think that next year the average salary of national league baseball players will be $383,000. Although we have a great athlete, Mr. St-Jean, among us, I think that those guys may be a bit overpaid. One thing is certain, Mr. Speaker, the people here work almost round the clock first to get elected but foremost to try and improve the lot of those whom they represent.
Imagine, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Prime Minister will get to be paid-the Prime Minister is now paid $67,000 and the Leader of the Opposition $53,000 and yet there are welders, as I was saying, who earn $1,300 a week and who are on strike because they want $2,000-as I was saying the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition will get substantially less than that despite the fact that their responsibilities are considerably greater. I think that in 1981 we have to be able to face facts and to make it possible for members of Parliament to work within the system.
I would like to go back to the pension system, Mr. Speaker. I know a member-and I am serious-who, when he came here, drove a Jaguar. Today he drives a small foreign car. Some members here were set up in practice and doing really well, their businesses were flourishing, but now they cannot do both, that is work as a member of Parliament and maintain their law practice or their business. What is wrong with wanting some security? A lawyer who leaves a good practice and who spends 10 or 15 years of his life here would have great difficulty, if he was defeated, adjusting and building up a clientele in order to enjoy the same standard of living he had before entering politics. To those who argue that the salaries of $40,000 proposed here today are indecent, I would say that some of our provincial counterparts earn more. In Quebec, for example, MLAs will be getting $49,000 as of next September.
I also remind the House that we recently voted a salary increase for judges which made their salaries jump from $50,000 to $72,000 a year. Why? Because we know they need it to do their job. There is nothing dishonest in that. There is

July 9, 1981
Senate and House of Commons Act nothing wrong in wanting a decent salary because decent salary helps one to do one's job and I think that the people who voted us into office expect from us first rate work.
We could give numerous examples. In the labour force and among professionals salaries are considerably higher than the one proposed here today. If I were to figure out the hourly salary of a member of Parliament, I am sure that some provinces would consider it illegal because it would be less than minimum wage. Of course, some will say: In my riding, my MP is not worth that much! This is what I would like to tell the people: Do you know how much your MP costs you? Your MP costs you about 25 to 30 cents a year. If my colleagues feel they are not worth 25 cents, I wonder what they are doing here. They have no respect for their constituents if they feel they are not worth a quarter.
Considering that, the work of a member is far from being an easy one. My hon. colleagues from the east should consider for a moment that our western friends have to log six hours of flying time to come and sit here five days a week and then go back to their ridings to carry on their work there. Think of our friends from the other provinces who have two homes and have to bring up their children by telephone. Yes, that is right: several hon. members in this House raise their families over the phone. That is how their families are raised.
I ask the people to think of that, to have a second look at the role and work of members of parliament. I say to the Canadian people that it is no easy task for us to sit here in judgment and vote ourselves an increase, being both our own judges and employers. It is no easy job and that is why it was decided to have an independent commission look into the whole problem. That commission recommended an increase spread over a three-year period to up to $45,000. After discussions with all the parties, it was decided, not because of the present political situation, not because it was feared we would not get re-elected, but because of the economic situation, to reduce that proposal by a third. And here again I say: those who maintain that two thirds of that increase today, as opposed to three thirds in three years from now, is a better proposition, are wrong. I beg of them to figure it out. The last proposal represents a net decrease of 26 per cent as compared with the recommendation of the independent Mclsaac-Balcer Commission. That is what it boils down to. In other words, today we are accepting a cut in salary. Had I been there, had I still been president of the union, I would never have accepted a cut in salary for the union members I was representing. I would not be ashamed to go to my constituents and to tell them: "Yes, ladies and gentlemen, I took part in the debate, because I thought I was worth that much money and if you do not agree, since we live in a democratic country, when the time comes, I am sure that you will know what to do."
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask all my colleagues, all those who are against this bill, to stop believing that everyone here is rich or a millionaire. Already in our
constituencies, some people think that we earn $50,000, $60,000 or $70,000 per year. In addition, seven years ago, when a bill was introduced to provide for a salary increase, some people thought that we had got three increases. The bill had been tabled on first reading and the next day it was mentioned in the newspapers, so there was the first increase. A second increase on second reading and when the vote was taken on third reading, they believed that a third increase had been granted.
I say to those same people that, since 1974 when the last increase was granted, hon. members' income has in fact increased by 4.4 per cent. Such are the facts. In a democratic society for professional and labour groups some catching up is in order and it was done. It is merely a slight catching up. 1 thank the Opposition House leaders. I thank the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) who did a lot of work on this. I also thank all my colleagues, especially the member for Quebec East (Mr. Duquet) for his efforts to come up with what I consider a decent minimum salary which will enable us to carry out some decent work and not to "fill our pockets", as some people suggest but on the contrary to continue to provide first rate service to those who have put their trust in us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very difficult debate for any member to intervene in. I think those of us who have been here for several years ought to take a moment to reflect that we have been through this before. The Hon. Mitchell Sharp, as president of the Privy Council, introduced a similar type of bill on December 17, 1974, and he said at that time:
-one of the most distasteful tasks for any minister is to take the lead in proposing a bill which, among other things, increases his own salary as a member of parliament and as a minister.
He was followed in that debate by a member who is well remembered and revered in this House, the great Ged Baldwin, who preceded the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) as the House leader for the Conservatives, and he said at that time:
We are faced here with a vexing, difficult and contentious problem, that of how to persuade people to come to this House or to become members of legislatures and do the job that they should do.
Mr. Baldwin at that point added:
All over the world the light of freedom is flickering in face of the strong winds of violence and intimidation, of attempts to secure a government of the people by other than democratic means. Let us not delude ourselves.
I see the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) is here tonight. He made a distinguished contribution to that debate, which continued on into the early part of the next year, and he said at that time:
-I suppose no member of parliament is likely to earn the undying favour of the public by speaking in favour of this bill, but the act is that the bill as it is now before us, and with possible future modifications, is not only one which would provide justice to hon. members of this House and the other place but it is also a bill which would safeguard the public interest.
July 9, 1981

That is what this debate is about today, the public interest.
There are only a few moments left in this debate. I hope the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) will have an opportunity to make his contribution. In speaking to support this bill I only want to tell the government House leader that it is time members of Parliament ended this business of having to stand in the House to speak about and vote on a subject of such clearly vested interest. It is time for the government to be serious about bringing in a measure that would enable the setting up of an independent tribunal following an election, not just a tribunal of former members to advise and recommend as the Mclsaac-Balcer report does, which report I support.
I think the government House leader, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) have done a distinguished job in bringing to this House the recommendation that we will vote on in a few moments, a recommendation which is two thirds of the Mclsaac-Balcer report. I say it is time members of Parliament stopped having to vote on such a measure in which they have a vested interest. Let us have a tribunal empowered to set the standards for future parliamentarians. That is what we need. I suggest to you, sir, and the other distinguished leaders in this Parliament that we need a tribunal headed by a judge, and will include a representative of labour, of management, a former parliamentarian and perhaps others, whatever is considered appropriate.
This tribunal would be empowered by a future Parliament to set the standard, and we would no longer have this distasteful job. It is not a pleasant thing for members to have to rise in this debate. I spoke to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton privately about this measure and he knows where I stand. I come here now and say publicly in support of what I said to him privately as a member of this House for nine years, with some experience, and as a father of five children, three of whom were in college at the same time, and as one who attempts to devote his full time to being a member of Parliament, but as one who does not dare to complain. I consider it an honour to walk onto this floor every day that Parliament is assembled. However, at the same time we have to recognize the realities of life.
I say to you, sir, it is absolutely essential that members of Parliament can continue to come here in a full-time capacity and not have to depend on previously acquired wealth in order to maintain their existence in this place. This, sir, is a place of the commoners. A former leader of this party, the great Robert Stanfield, used to say: "You have to remember, this is a place of the commoners". I say to you, Mr. Speaker, if you want that to continue, you must enable people of ordinary means to come into this establishment and stay here.
I think this reasonable proposition put forward tonight by the combined endeavours of the House leaders has enabled us to come to this point where we are about to vote, and as distasteful as this voters, let us proceed with it. I am looking down the road to a younger generation and I want people to be
Senate and House of Commons Act
able to come in here, people who have some beliefs and who want to be able to stay here. I think it is absolutely essential for world order, for the wellbeing of Canadians and for the democratic system that we have a system of fair compensation, which is not by any means rewarding-and we know that the Mclsaac-Balcer recommendations are not rewarding; they are compensatory. We say it is essential to maintain that kind of fair, equitable and stable system, not on behalf of the members who happen to be here now, but for those who will be here in the future. That is the reason I have come here tonight to make this address.
